content.text:
Done — the media echo issue is fixed across all three layers, committed `8a1c5835` on `fix/media-echo`.

## What landed
**Layer 1 — Renderer echo guards (now latency-proof)**
- GTK: `should_seek` now compares a `MEDIA_POSITION` write against the renderer's **last-reported** position (`MediaPlayer.last_reported`), not `currentTime` — a network-delayed echo is recognized at any latency, so it never seeks.
- TS: `apply.ts` — `MEDIA_POSITION` within `0.25 s` of `lastReported` and `MEDIA_VOLUME` within `0.01` of `lastReportedVolume` are skipped (added `lastReportedVolume` tracking).

**Layer 2 — Demo decoupling (the correct architecture)**
- `Audio` gained `onPositionReport`/`onVolumeReport`: `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED`/`MEDIA_VOLUME_CHANGED` flow to the **display** signals, while `MEDIA_POSITION`/`MEDIA_VOLUME` stay bound to user-only **command** signals (`seekRequest`/`volumeRequest`).
- The seek/volume sliders present the display and write the command on drag (`SeekControl`/`VolumeControl`); prev/next + ended reset both.
- Regression test: a `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` emits **no** `MEDIA_POSITION`.

**Layer 3 — Spec** (`spec/EVENTS.md` Media): commands vs reports MUST be decoupled, and renderers MUST skip a command write matching the last reported value.

## Verified
`cargo test` 30 suites; `npm test` 182 + typecheck; full `mvn` reactor tests green (pathland-view 100, demo-views 17, render-html, gtk-demo, server-core). Status files updated for render-gtk, lib/typescript, pathland-view, and the demo.

## Objective
- Fix the **media-position echo loop** (audio seek jitter) on branch `fix/media-echo` (created from `main` @ `69409f1b`): the demo binds `MEDIA_POSITION` to the same `position` signal that `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` feeds, so every second the network-delayed echo seeks the player backward. User approved: **all three layers (renderer guard GTK+TS, Java demo decoupling, spec) + also volume**.

## Important Details
- Echo loop confirmed: renderer reports `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` ~1/s → `position.set` → re-emits `SET_PROPERTY MEDIA_POSITION` → renderer seek guard `|currentTime − target| > 0.25` fails when network delay > 0.25 s → per-second seek jitter.
- Fix semantics: guard compares against the renderer's **last-reported** position (echo ≈ lastReported, suppressed at any latency; real seeks still fire; only a no-op seek within 0.25 s of the report is suppressed). Same pattern for volume (epsilon 0.01).
- GTK does **not** emit `MEDIA_VOLUME_CHANGED` (no volume echo on desktop) — the volume guard is web-only; the demo's hidden `<audio>` has no native controls, so the volume decoupling is defensive.
- Decoupling design: `Audio.position(signal)` = MEDIA_POSITION **command** binding; new `Audio.onPositionReport(signal)` = MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED **report** sink (defaults to the position signal for backward compat). Same for volume. `AudioStyle.Configuration` exposes the command signals (`config.position()`/`config.volume()`).
- Demo sliders need display+command on one signal: `SeekControl` (presents `position`, drag writes `position`+`seekRequest`) wrapped by `PercentSeek`; `VolumeControl` (presents `volume`, drag writes `volume`+`volumeRequest`). Prev/next/ended must reset both `position` and `seekRequest` to 0.
- Standing workflow: assistant commits on feature branches only; the user merges via GitHub PRs themselves (PRs #112–#116 merged so far); no push/merge by the assistant. The user handles the merge; the user's earlier "commit only" directive evolved into "I'll handle the merge".
- 6 original MP3s remain untracked at the repo root (user's source files; not committed): `Building_on_Solid_Ground.mp3`, `Pathland_Crossing.mp3`, `Rendered_Free.mp3`, `Rendered_In_Your_Arms.mp3`, `Sixty_Frames_Per_Second.mp3`, `The_Pathland_Dream.mp3`.

## Work State
### Completed
- This task (`fix/media-echo`, **Layer 1 + part of Layer 2 done**):
  - GTK `pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs`: `MediaPlayer` gained `last_reported: Rc<Cell<f32>>` (stored in both constructors in `create_media_player`); seek guard now `should_seek(player.last_reported.get() as f64, target)` (line ~656) instead of querying `currentTime`; `should_seek` doc updated. `cargo test -p pathland-render-gtk` → 49 green (existing `should_seek` tests were already symmetric).
  - TS `lib/typescript/src/apply.ts`: media state gained `lastReportedVolume`; `volumechange` listener records `state.lastReportedVolume`; `PROP_MEDIA_POSITION` guard now `Math.abs(reported - target) > 0.25` with `reported = state.lastReported`; `PROP_MEDIA_VOLUME` guard `reported < 0 || |reported - target| > 0.01`; added test-only export `__setMediaLastReported(el, seconds)`. Test `seeks only on a meaningful MEDIA_POSITION change` updated (calls `setupMediaElement(wrapper, r)` first, sets `lastReported=3`, `currentTime=3.5`). `npm test` → 182 green; typecheck clean.
  - Java DSL `lib/java/pathland-view/src/main/java/com/pathland/view/Audio.java`: added `reportPosition`/`reportVolume` fields, `onPositionReport(...)`/`onVolumeReport(...)` methods (all 8 constructor call sites updated); `mediaInput.onTimeUpdated`/`onVolumeChanged` write the report sink when set, else the bound signal.
  - Demo: created `lib/java/pathland-demo-views/src/main/java/com/pathland/demo/music/SeekControl.java` and `VolumeControl.java`; `MusicPlayerView.java` now declares `State<Float> seekRequest` + `volumeRequest` and passes 6 signals to `PlayerBar`.
- Earlier finished workstreams (all merged to `main`, currently `69409f1b`): alignment overhaul (`dd4f191f`, `91b3e962`), system fonts (`25fc23d7`, `a1b03a75`), ratatui renderer on unmerged `feat/ratatui-renderer` (`fa62845e`, `787bbe68`, `9a3634d3`), in-flight interaction suppression (`35ede98a`, PR #113), WS send-recovery (`235b6035`, PR #114), asset dedup + 128k mono (`c65baf23`), Quarkus disk asset serving (`758b3f7e`, `319338b2`), Spring asset serving via `pathland.asset-dir` in `PathlandIndexController` (`de004dc5`, PR #116).
- Created GitHub issue **#117** "WS transport reliability: built-in ACK (frame sequencing, replay buffer, event retransmit, liveness)" on milestone **"Enterprise SRE · HTMX & BFF replacement"** (not implemented, per user).

### Active
- `fix/media-echo` branch in progress: **`PlayerBar.java` and `PlayerControlsStyle.java` not yet rewired** to the decoupled signals.
- Not yet done: demo decoupling test (`timeUpdatesDoNotEchoAsMediaPosition` — mount → `dispatcher.dispatch(Event.mediaTimeUpdated(...))` → assert the emitted delta contains **no** `MEDIA_POSITION`; existing `anySetProperty`/`hasProperty` helpers check specific values, a `anyProperty(frame, prop)` helper may be needed); **Layer 3 spec** (`spec/EVENTS.md` Media: `MEDIA_POSITION`/`MEDIA_VOLUME` are commands, `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED`/`MEDIA_VOLUME_CHANGED` are reports; apps MUST NOT bind a command to its report signal; renderers MUST suppress a write within an epsilon of the last-reported value); status.md updates (render-gtk, lib/typescript, pathland-view, pathland-demo-views); full verify (`cargo test`, `npm test`+typecheck, `mvn -q clean install` + demo tests); commit on `fix/media-echo`.

### Blocked
- None. (The existing `MusicPlayerViewTest.mediaEventsDriveThePlayerState` should still pass since `onTimeUpdated`/`onVolumeChanged` route to the report sinks.)

## Next Move
1. Rewire `PlayerBar.java`: constructor gains `seekRequest`, `volumeRequest`; `Audio.of(...).position(seekRequest).onPositionReport(position).volume(volumeRequest).onVolumeReport(volume)`; pass all 6 signals to `PlayerControlsStyle`; `ended()` resets both `position` and `seekRequest`.
2. Rewire `PlayerControlsStyle.java`: `of(trackIndex, position, seekRequest, volume, volumeRequest)`; seek slider = `Slider.of(new PercentSeek(new SeekControl(position, seekRequest), duration), 0f, 100f)`; volume slider = `Slider.of(new VolumeControl(volume, volumeRequest), 0f, 1f)`; prev/next reset `position` + `config.position()` (seekRequest) to 0.
3. Add the demo decoupling test (time update emits no `MEDIA_POSITION`) in `MusicPlayerViewTest`.
4. Add Layer 3 spec contract to `spec/EVENTS.md` Media; update status.md files.
5. Verify (`cargo test`, `npm test`+typecheck, `mvn -q clean install` + demo-views tests) and commit on `fix/media-echo`; user merges.

# Pathland Java server runtime — WebSocket delta dead-stop investigation

## Executive summary

There is **no heartbeat/ping/keepalive anywhere in server-core** (verified: the only matches for `alive|PONG|ping|keepalive` were unrelated log strings). All server→client deltas are **purely event-driven**: a signal `set()` synchronously flushes binding effects on the registry's single actor thread, the emitter produces a frame, `FrameOpcodeSink.endFrame()` appends it to a `DeltaBatcher`, and the batcher flushes on a 20 ms daemon timer or 16 KB threshold. There are exactly two threads per registry: the actor and the batcher's scheduler. **Several concrete, silent-dead-stop paths exist**, the most likely being: (1) a single send failure permanently detaches the session from its still-open Spring WebSocket (nothing ever closes it → client never reconnects), (2) a blocking send on the batcher thread that stalls the shared batcher monitor and thereby the actor thread, and (3) a binding effect that throws once and permanently loses its signal subscriptions.

## 1. PathlandSession — lifecycle, drain, thread, exception handling

File: `/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/com/pathland/server/PathlandSession.java`

- **No thread of its own.** The session is pure logic; all signal writes, dispatches, and `endFrame` calls run on the registry's **actor thread** (`PathlandRegistry.java:48-52`). The only executor it owns is the batcher's daemon scheduler (`DeltaBatcher.java:61-65`).
- **Drain path (the "eager signal" pipeline), all synchronous on the actor:**
  - A signal write (e.g. `count.update(...)` from a tap action, `InputDispatcher.java:58`) → `WritableSignalImpl.set` (`WritableSignalImpl.java:28-36`) → `propagate()` → effects scheduled and **flushed synchronously** in the global static `Scheduler` (`Scheduler.java:26-40`).
  - The node binding effect body calls `sink.beginFrame(); sink.setText(...); sink.endFrame();` (`Emitter.java:291-299`).
  - The session **overrides `endFrame`** (`PathlandSession.java:86-101`): calls `super.endFrame()`, then — only if `connection != null && connection.isOpen()` — appends the frame to the `DeltaBatcher`.
  - The batcher flushes on its daemon scheduler (20 ms, `DeltaBatcher.java:39,82-83`) or inline at 16 KB (`DeltaBatcher.java:80-81`).
- **Mount frame is deliberately dropped** (comment at `PathlandSession.java:88-92`): `connection` is null during the constructor, so `endFrame` sees `conn == null` and returns. The connection is wired only via `connect()` (`PathlandSession.java:129-131`) after mount.
- **`resync()`** (`PathlandSession.java:134-137`): `emitter.renderFull()` then `batcher.flush()` — runs on the actor, sends immediately.
- **Exception handling in `dispatch`** (`PathlandSession.java:176-182`): a `RuntimeException` from the signal flush is **caught and logged** ("dropping event batch"). The actor thread survives, but see §6-A for what the exception left behind.

For Spring this means the underlying WebSocket is never closed after a send failure → the client sees an open socket forever (see §6-C).
- **Timers:** none in the session. `applyEnvironment` (`PathlandSession.java:118-126`) is not a timer — it's a signal write triggered by an inbound WS `META::ENVIRONMENT` message.
- **`close()`** (`PathlandSession.java:205-210`): `state.close()`, `emitter.destroy()`, `batcher.close()`, `connection = null`.

## 2. PathlandConnection — the send seam

Interface: `/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/com/pathland/server/PathlandConnection.java:8-15` — just `send(byte[])` + `isOpen()`.

- **Spring adapter** — `/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-starter/src/main/java/com/pathland/spring/SpringConnection.java:17-28`:
  - `send` → `session.sendMessage(new BinaryMessage(bytes))`, wrapping failures in `RuntimeException`. Spring's `StandardWebSocketSession.sendMessage` is internally synchronized but **can block** when the container's outbound buffer fills on a slow/half-dead client, and throws on a broken pipe.
  - No queue, no backpressure, **no close-on-failure at this layer** (only `isOpen()` → `session.isOpen()`, which stays `true` for a half-open connection).
  - **Not `AutoCloseable`** → `closeConnection` is a no-op for it (§1).
- **Quarkus adapter** — `/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-quarkus-starter/src/main/java/com/pathland/quarkus/QuarkusConnection.java:20-66`:
  - Serialized async sends (`ConcurrentLinkedQueue` + `AtomicBoolean sending`, `QuarkusConnection.java:23-24,45-65`); at most one `sendBinary` subscription in flight.
  - On failure: `failed = true` + `connection.close()` (`QuarkusConnection.java:59-64`). **The javadoc at `QuarkusConnection.java:16-18` names the exact symptom you're chasing**: *"the remote seekbar symptom: the browser suddenly stops receiving deltas"*.
  - **Residual risk**: if the `sendBinary` future **never completes** (half-dead connection where neither success nor failure fires), `sending` stays `true` forever and `drain()` never resumes — the connection remains "open" and silently delivers nothing (`QuarkusConnection.java:54-65`).

## 3. DeltaBatcher — batching policy and stuck-batch analysis

File: `/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/com/pathland/server/DeltaBatcher.java`

- Policy: flush every **20 ms** (`DEFAULT_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MILLIS`, line 39) or when the merged batch ≥ **16 KB** (`DEFAULT_MAX_BATCH_BYTES`, line 41), whichever first; single pending flush guarded by `AtomicBoolean flushScheduled` (line 50).
- `append` (lines 69-85) and `flush` (lines 88-98) are **both `synchronized` on the batcher instance**. Note that the `sender` consumer runs **inside the lock** (`flush`, line 97) — this is the crux of the blocking hazard below.
- Two threads call the sender:
  - the **scheduler daemon thread** (timer flush, `scheduler.schedule(this::flush, ...)`, line 83);
  - the **actor thread** (inline byte-threshold flush inside `append`, lines 80-81; and `resync()`'s immediate `batcher.flush()`, `PathlandSession.java:136`).
- **Stuck-batch scenarios:**
  - **Blocking sender stalls everything.** `conn.send` (Spring's blocking `sendMessage`) runs while holding the batcher monitor. If it blocks (full TCP send buffer, slow client), the **scheduler thread** is stuck in `flush`, and the **actor thread's next `append` blocks on the monitor** (`DeltaBatcher.java:69`) → every session on that registry stops processing both events and deltas.
  - **One-shot timer is not re-armed after a no-op flush is fine** — every append below threshold re-arms via CAS; no lost-wakeup in the normal interleaving (verified by tracing all orderings of the synchronized `append`/`flush`).
  - **`close()`** (`DeltaBatcher.java:101-103`) calls `scheduler.shutdownNow()` — a pending scheduled flush is cancelled and unflushed opcodes are discarded, but this only happens during session teardown.
  - If `scheduler.schedule` (line 83) throws `RejectedExecutionException` after the CAS already set `flushScheduled = true` (session being closed concurrently), the batch is stuck — but the connection is being torn down anyway, so it is not your symptom.
  - If `sender.accept` throws an `Error` (not `Exception`) on the scheduler thread, the batch is lost; `flushScheduled` was already reset (line 89), so the next append re-arms. Recoverable.

## 4. PathlandRegistry — 1:1 lifecycle, eviction, timeout

File: `/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/com/pathland/server/PathlandRegistry.java`

- **No eviction, no timeout, no TTL.** Sessions live in `ConcurrentHashMap<String, PathlandSession> sessions` (line 54) until `close(sessionId)` (lines 183-191), `shutdown()` (lines 194-201), or replaced by a new connection with the same `uiId` in `open` (lines 152-160). A session whose socket silently dies without a close callback **leaks forever** (its batcher scheduler keeps running; its `endFrame` keeps dropping frames because `isOpen()` may still return true or the send keeps throwing).
- Single actor thread (`Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor`, lines 48-52) serializes `open`/`environment`/`dispatch`/`resync`/`close`. Tasks that throw are swallowed by the executor (printed to stderr) and the thread continues — **but** if the throwing task is the lazy session creation (`session()`, lines 204-217, invoked from `environment`/`dispatch`), the session is never put in `sessions`, the pending connection is consumed (line 207), and **every subsequent message silently retries and fails** — no deltas ever flow after that.
- `dispatch` silently drops any inbound batch > 64 KB (`MAX_EVENT_BATCH`, lines 41, 170-172) — a dropped event is not a dead-stop but can look like the app stopped reacting to one specific input.
- Session creation happens inside `session()` on the actor: `new PathlandSession(...)` runs `app.newRoot().render(env)` and `emitter.mount(...)` (`PathlandSession.java:109-113`); any throw there takes down the whole `environment`/`dispatch` task silently.

## 5. Periodic tasks / scheduled executors / watchers

Only two threads exist per registry, and **neither is a periodic watcher**:

- `"pathland-actor"` — single-thread executor, event-driven only (`PathlandRegistry.java:48-52`).
- `"pathland-delta-batcher"` — single-thread **daemon** scheduled executor per session (`DeltaBatcher.java:46,61-65`), used only for the 20 ms coalescing flush. No `scheduleAtFixedRate`/`scheduleWithFixedDelay` anywhere in the Java stack (verified by grep across `lib/java`).

There is **no environment ticking, no signal re-emission loop, no watchdog**. The global synchronous signal `Scheduler` (`/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-view/src/main/java/com/pathland/view/signal/Scheduler.java:13-14`) is a **static** queue with a **static** `flushing` flag, shared by every session in every registry in the JVM. It flushes to quiescence at the end of the outermost signal write, on whatever thread calls `set()`. Two consequences worth flagging:

- The SSR request thread performs a signal write inside the session constructor: `applyEnvironment(env)` → `activePath.set(env.route())` (`PathlandSession.java:114` and `PathlandSession.java:118-119`). This flushes the **global** effect queue, which can contain **live sessions' effects**, running them on the **request thread** while the actor thread also runs them → the `FrameOpcodeSink` (not synchronized; `FrameOpcodeSink.java:20-23`) can be mutated concurrently → corrupt frames or exceptions.
- If any effect self-referentially writes a signal it reads and the value changes each write, `Scheduler.flush` spins forever with `flushing = true` (lines 26-40); the actor blocks forever and **every other session in the JVM stops flushing** (their `schedule()` calls return early at line 27-28).

## 6. Silent dead-stop candidates (ranked by likelihood)

### A. A binding effect throws once → permanently loses its subscriptions (HIGH)
In `Effect.runIfScheduled` (`/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-view/src/main/java/com/pathland/view/signal/Effect.java:28-49`):
- `resetProducers()` (line 39) drops **all** producer edges **before** `fn.run()` (line 41); new edges are re-recorded only as the body reads its signals.
- If `fn.run()` throws, `error` is cached and an `EffectException` is rethrown (lines 43-45). The effect's producer list is now empty or partial → it is **never again in any signal's `consumers` list** → future `signal.set()` never marks it dirty → **that binding silently never fires again**. The rethrown `EffectException` propagates through `Scheduler.flush` → `WritableSignalImpl.set` → the tap/input action → `InputDispatcher.dispatch` (`InputDispatcher.java:48-108`) → caught in `PathlandSession.dispatch` (`PathlandSession.java:176-182`) and logged as "dropping event batch".

This affects every binding registered in `Emitter.registerNodeBindings` (`Emitter.java:289-348`). In the counter demo, the *only* live delta is the text binding on `countLabel` (`CounterControls.java:23-25`); if that effect throws once (e.g. a computed body throwing, `ComputedSignal.java:41-73` caches and rethrows on every read), **all visible deltas stop** while the WS stays open.

The structural variant is worse: `Emitter.reconcileSlot` (`Emitter.java:357-420`) calls `destroySubtreeBindings(oldChildren)` and `forgetInputs(oldChildren)` at lines 376-377 **before** the new subtree is reconciled and re-registered at lines 413-419. A throw anywhere in between (e.g. `content.render(env)` at line 369) leaves the slot's bindings destroyed and the new subtree unregistered → the UI freezes after **one bad navigation/reconcile**, exactly "works, then stops."

### B. Blocking send stalls the batcher monitor → actor stalls (HIGH, remote/slow client)
`DeltaBatcher.flush` invokes the sender **inside the monitor** (`DeltaBatcher.java:97`). Spring's `session.sendMessage` (`SpringConnection.java:19`) can block indefinitely on a full outbound buffer (slow/minimized/half-dead client). The scheduler thread is stuck in `flush`; the actor thread's next `append` (`DeltaBatcher.java:69`) blocks on the same monitor → **all sessions on that registry stop** — inbound events stop being routed and outbound deltas stop. Client sees an open WS that never delivers.

### C. Send-failure drop with no close → permanent silent stall (HIGH, Spring)
`sendBatch` (`PathlandSession.java:145-157`) sets `connection = null` on any send exception. `closeConnection` (`PathlandSession.java:160-168`) is a no-op for `SpringConnection` (not `AutoCloseable`). So after a single transient send failure (a broken pipe that the container hasn't yet turned into a close callback, an `IllegalStateException`, etc.), the session permanently drops all future frames while **the underlying Spring WebSocket stays open**. The client's reconnect logic (`lib/typescript/src/transport.ts:110-121`) fires only on `onclose`/`onerror` — it never fires, no reconnect, no `META::RESYNC`, deltas stop forever. (Quarkus is hardened against this internally: `QuarkusConnection.java:59-64` closes on failure.)

### D. Synchronous Redis writes on the actor thread (MEDIUM-HIGH, "after a while")
Every `State` field adds a persist effect (`PersistentState.java:54-60`) that runs on the actor during **every** signal flush and performs a **blocking** Lettuce sync `commands.set` (`RedisStateStore.java:69-81`); session creation does a blocking `commands.get` (`RedisStateStore.java:52-66`). The RedisURI timeout is only the 2 s connect timeout (`RedisStateStore.java:40-43`); there is **no command timeout** (`RedisClient.setDefaultTimeout` is never called), so a Redis that hangs after startup (partition, GC, dropped connection with reconnect backoff) blocks the actor thread indefinitely → deltas stop everywhere on that registry. This matches "works at first, then stops" if Redis degrades.

### E. Infinite self-referential effect loop (MEDIUM, app-dependent)
An effect that writes a signal it reads, changing the value each time, spins `Scheduler.flush` (`Scheduler.java:32-36`) with the global `flushing=true` forever → actor blocked and the entire JVM's signal system wedged.

### F. Quarkus send future never completing (LOW-MEDIUM)
`QuarkusConnection.drain` (`QuarkusConnection.java:45-65`): if `sendBinary`'s future never completes, `sending` stays `true` and no further sends are drained; the connection stays open silently.

### G. Session creation throwing on the actor (LOW)
Lazy `session()` (`PathlandRegistry.java:204-217`) swallows construction failures (executor swallows the task exception) → session never registered, every subsequent message retries and fails silently; deltas never start (or restart) even though the WS is open.

## 7. Heartbeat / ping — none exists

Grep for `heartbeat|ping|keepalive|PONG|alive` across `pathland-server-core` returns **no protocol or transport heartbeat** (only an unrelated `"dropping event batch"` log and a `status.md` prose mention). The starters add none either. The TypeScript client reconnects only on socket `onclose`/`onerror` (`lib/typescript/src/transport.ts:110-121`) and requests `META::RESYNC` on reconnect (`transport.ts:95-105`), but **never probes liveness on a silent connection**. Consequently a half-open TCP connection (NAT/proxy idle timeout, laptop sleep, dead-but-unclosed peer) is undetectable by either side, which compounds every failure path above: no send ever fails loudly, no close ever fires, the client waits forever.

## Concrete recommendations (where to look first)

1. `PathlandSession.sendBatch`/`closeConnection` (`PathlandSession.java:145-168`) — make `SpringConnection` close the underlying session (or implement `AutoCloseable`) so a send failure surfaces as a close → client reconnects + RESYNCs instead of stalling.
2. `DeltaBatcher.flush` (`DeltaBatcher.java:88-98`) — move the `sender` call **outside** the monitor (copy the pending batch under lock, send after releasing) so a blocking `conn.send` can't stall the actor.
3. `Effect.runIfScheduled` (`Effect.java:39-45`) — don't `resetProducers()` before `fn.run()` (or restore producers on throw), so a throwing effect keeps its subscriptions and keeps retrying; and consider re-throwing to the registry so the session can be torn down deliberately.
4. `Emitter.reconcileSlot` (`Emitter.java:376-419`) — re-register bindings in a `finally` so a failed reconcile can't orphan the slot's bindings.
5. `RedisStateStore` (`RedisStateStore.java:35-49`) — set a real command timeout (`RedisClient.setDefaultTimeout`) and/or make persistence async, so a Redis hang can't block the actor.
6. Add a heartbeat (e.g. `META` ping) at both ends — there is currently no way to detect a half-open connection, which is the umbrella cause of the "open WebSocket that never delivers" symptom.

# Pathland SSR+WS Demo — WebSocket Endpoint & Server Config Investigation

This report covers both starters (`pathland-quarkus-starter`, `pathland-spring-boot-starter`), both demos, the shared server runtime (`pathland-server-core`), and the browser client (`lib/typescript`) since the delta path spans all of them.

---

## 1. WebSocket endpoint/handler classes and lifecycle handling

### Quarkus starter (`quarkus-websockets-next`)

**`pathland-quarkus-starter/src/main/java/com/pathland/quarkus/PathlandSocket.java`** — root app endpoint:

- `@WebSocket(path = "/_pathland/ws")` — **line 29**
- `@OnOpen void open()` — **lines 41–53**. Resolves the registry for `/`, unwraps the CDI session-scoped `WebSocketConnection` via `ClientProxy.unwrap(Arc.container().instance(WebSocketConnection.class).get())` (lines 50–51), then `registry.open(uiId(), windowId(), new QuarkusConnection(resolved))` (line 52).
- `@OnClose void close()` — **lines 55–61**: `registry.close(uiId())`.
- `@OnBinaryMessage void onBinary(byte[] message)` — **lines 63–78**: routes `META::RESYNC` → `registry.resync`, `META::ENVIRONMENT` → `registry.environment`, anything else → `registry.dispatch`.
- No `@OnError`, no `@OnTextMessage`, no `@OnPingMessage`/`@OnPongMessage` (the annotations exist in `io.quarkus.websockets.next` but are unused).

**`MountedPathlandSocket.java`** — same shape for mounted apps:
- `@WebSocket(path = "/{app}/_pathland/ws")` — **line 26**; `registry()` resolves the `{app}` path param once (lines 79–91). Same open/close/onBinary triple (lines 39–76). No `@OnError`/ping/pong handlers.

### Spring Boot starter (`spring-websocket`)

**`pathland-spring-boot-starter/src/main/java/com/pathland/spring/PathlandSocket.java`** — extends `AbstractWebSocketHandler`:

- **`afterConnectionEstablished`** (lines 43–48): resolves `ConnectionIds` (fresh `uiId` + `wid` from the handshake URI), stores in a `ConcurrentHashMap`, calls `registry.open(...)`.
- **`handleMessage`** (lines 50–64): only `BinaryMessage` is handled; text/ping/pong frames are silently ignored (they fall through to `AbstractWebSocketHandler` defaults — which for a `PingMessage` does auto-echo a Pong, for `PongMessage` is a no-op).
- **`afterConnectionClosed`** (lines 66–69) → `close(session)` (lines 76–81): removes ids and calls `registry.close(uiId)`.
- **`handleTransportError`** (lines 71–74): also calls `close(session)`.
- Registration: **`PathlandAutoConfiguration.java:83-86`**:
  ```java
  registry.addHandler(new PathlandSocket(r), r.base() + "/ws").setAllowedOrigins("*")
  ```
  No `setMaxSessionIdleTimeout`, no buffer-size limits, no interceptors, no `addEndpoint` custom configurator.

### Shared server runtime (`pathland-server-core`)

- **`PathlandRegistry`** (`PathlandRegistry.java`) — sessions keyed 1:1 by a per-connection `uiId`; all session work serialized on a **single daemon actor thread** (`Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor`, lines 48–52, thread name `"pathland-actor"`).
  - `open` (152–160) registers a `PendingSession`; the real `PathlandSession` is created **lazily on the first inbound message** (`environment`, 163–166; `dispatch`, 169–175; `resync`, 178–180 → `session()`, 204–217) and the pending connection is wired with `session.connect(pending.connection())` (line 212).
  - `close` (183–191) closes the session and drops the pending connection.

---

## 2. Idle timeout / maxSessionIdleTimeout / maxIdleTimeout settings

**Nothing is configured anywhere in the Pathland code.** Verified by repo-wide grep for `setMaxSessionIdleTimeout`, `maxIdleTimeout`, `idle-timeout`, `setMaxBinaryMessageBufferSize`, `setMaxTextMessageBufferSize`, `server.websocket`, `http.max-connections`, `undertow`, `vertx`, etc. — **zero matches** in `lib/java` and `lib/typescript`.

What the containers actually default to (verified against the local Maven jars):

- **Spring/Tomcat**: `tomcat-embed-websocket` `WsWebSocketContainer` initializes `defaultMaxSessionIdleTimeout` to **`-1`** (decompiled constructor: `ldc2_w -1l; putfield defaultMaxSessionIdleTimeout`), i.e. no idle timeout. Spring Boot 3.5.16 / Tomcat 10.1.x.
- **Quarkus/Vert.x**: `quarkus-websockets-next` exposes only `quarkus.websockets-next.server.max-frame-size` / `max-message-size` (default 65536); **no idle-timeout config item exists** in `WebSocketsServerRuntimeConfig`. Vert.x adds a Netty `IdleStateHandler` from `quarkus.http.idle-timeout` (default 30 s), but on HTTP/1.1 configuration the handler is **removed from the pipeline** (`HttpServerWorker$1.configure`: `pipeline.remove(idle)`), so an upgraded WebSocket is not subject to it.
- Quarkus version 3.39.1, Spring Boot 3.5.16 (parent `lib/java/pom.xml:41-42`).

So the server will not idle-close the socket on its own — any idle timeout is coming from a **proxy/load-balancer/NAT in front of the app**, not from the app.

---

## 3. Ping/pong keepalive handling

**No application-level keepalive exists on either side.**

- **Server**: neither `PathlandSocket` (Quarkus) nor `PathlandSocket` (Spring) declares ping/pong handlers or calls `sendPing`/`sendPong`. Quarkus's `Sender` interface has `sendPing(Buffer)`/`sendPong(Buffer)` (verified in the jar) but nothing calls them. Vert.x/Netty and Spring/Tomcat both auto-echo an *inbound* client ping at the protocol level, but **nothing sends periodic pings**.
- **Client** (`lib/typescript/src/transport.ts`): no ping, no `setInterval` watchdog, no heartbeat. The client only reconnects when `onclose` fires (lines 114–123). `onerror` (110–113) does nothing ("onclose always follows"). `transport.open` is just `readyState === 1` (lines 68–70) — **a half-dead connection still reports `open: true`**, so every input handler in `index.ts` (gated on `transport.open`, e.g. lines 227, 256, 285, 312, 368, 390, 442) keeps "sending" into a dead socket that the browser will not notice for a long time (no close frame ever arrives, no TCP keepalive at the app layer).

---

## 4. OnClose / onError handling — does anything close the session silently?

### Quarkus endpoint
No `@OnError`. If `onBinary` throws (e.g. a malformed batch from `FrameCodec.decodeEnvironment`), Quarkus's connector error handler runs — the starter never participates in it. `@OnClose` only unregisters the session.

### Spring endpoint
`handleTransportError` (lines 71–74) → `close(session)` → `registry.close(uiId())`. So a transport error *is* cleaned up server-side. But note the client is only notified if a close frame actually makes it out.

### The important silent-close path — `PathlandSession.sendBatch`
**`PathlandSession.java:145-168`**:
```java
private void sendBatch(byte[] bytes) {
    PathlandConnection conn = connection;
    if (conn == null || !conn.isOpen()) {
        connection = null;
        return;
    }
    try {
        conn.send(bytes);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        connection = null;
        closeConnection(conn);        // line 155
    }
}

private static void closeConnection(PathlandConnection conn) {   // lines 160-168
    if (conn instanceof AutoCloseable closeable) { ... }
}
```
- **`SpringConnection` is NOT `AutoCloseable`** (`implements PathlandConnection` only, line 8) and has no `close()` method. **`QuarkusConnection` is also NOT `AutoCloseable`** (line 20).
- Therefore `closeConnection` is a **no-op for both adapters**. For Spring, a failed `session.sendMessage` (wrapped into `RuntimeException` at `SpringConnection.java:20-22`) nulls the session's `connection` and **never closes the Spring `WebSocketSession`, never sends a close frame, never notifies the client**. The browser keeps an "open" socket; every later delta is silently dropped at `endFrame` (lines 93–96: `conn == null` → return). **This is a permanent silent stall with no reconnect, no RESYNC.**

The Quarkus adapter handles the failure more explicitly — on `sendBinary` failure it sets `failed = true` and calls `connection.close()` (`QuarkusConnection.java:59-65`), intending the client to reconnect + RESYNC. But the close subscription swallows errors (`.with(ignored2 -> {}, ignored2 -> {})`, line 64): if the connection is already dead (proxy half-close), the close frame can't be delivered either, and the client still never sees it.

There is also a Quarkus-specific **stall-inside-the-adapter**: `QuarkusConnection.drain()` (lines 45–66) only allows one `sendBinary` subscription in flight. If the Uni **neither completes nor fails** (a half-dead connection where the write hangs), `sending` stays `true` forever, `pending` accumulates, and all future `send` calls return immediately (line 46–48). No error, no close, no delivery — silent stall on an "open" socket.

---

## 5. Push seam — how PathlandSession/DeltaBatcher is wired to the WS endpoint

The push path is **entirely off the WebSocket I/O thread**:

1. A signal change (e.g. `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` from the browser → `InputDispatcher` → app signal `set`) runs the emitter's node-binding effects, which call `FrameOpcodeSink.endFrame` — overridden in `PathlandSession` to append the frame to the `DeltaBatcher` (**PathlandSession.java:85-102**, batcher at line 46, constructed at line 103).
2. **`DeltaBatcher`** (`DeltaBatcher.java`) coalesces frames and flushes on a **per-session daemon scheduler thread** (`"pathland-delta-batcher"`, lines 61–65) every `DEFAULT_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MILLIS = 20` ms (line 39) or `DEFAULT_MAX_BATCH_BYTES = 16 KiB` (line 41).
3. `flush()` (**lines 88–98**) calls `sender.accept(FrameCodec.encodeFrame(merged))` — the `sender` is `PathlandSession::sendBatch`, which calls `conn.send(bytes)` **on the batcher scheduler thread**, while holding the batcher's monitor (both `append` and `flush` are `synchronized` on the batcher, lines 69/88).
4. `conn.send` resolves to:
   - **Quarkus** (`QuarkusConnection.send`, lines 31–38): queue + async `sendBinary(...).subscribe()` — non-blocking, failures handled on the Vert.x callback thread.
   - **Spring** (`SpringConnection.send`, lines 16–23): **synchronous, blocking `session.sendMessage`** on the batcher thread. Spring's `StandardWebSocketSession.sendMessage` is internally locked, and the batcher lock serializes all sends per session, so concurrency isn't the issue — but any `IOException`/`IllegalStateException` becomes a `RuntimeException` that triggers the silent-stall path in §4.

**Key risk**: the write happens on a *non-WebSocket* thread (the batcher scheduler). An exception is caught in `sendBatch`, so it never kills the scheduler — but for Spring it leaves a dead-session-with-live-socket state, and for Quarkus a hung subscription leaves a live-session-with-dead-queue state. Neither produces any client-visible signal.

Also note `resync()` (**PathlandSession.java:134-137**) calls `batcher.flush()` directly on the **actor thread** (`PathlandRegistry.resync` → actor, line 179) — so `flush`/`sendBatch` can run on the actor thread too; still serialized via the batcher lock, still off the WS thread.

---

## 6. Demo application.properties (both, complete)

### Quarkus demo — `pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/application.properties` (14 lines, quoted in full)

**No `quarkus.http.websocket` / `quarkus.websockets-next.*` / vertx / idle-timeout / max-connections settings of any kind.** (`pathland.debug-html` is commented out.)

### Spring Boot demo — `pathland-spring-boot-demo/src/main/resources/application.properties` (9 lines)

# Cache the static resources ...
spring.web.resources.cache.period=7d
```
**No `server.websocket.*`, no `server.tomcat.*`, no timeout settings.** The `target/classes/application.properties` copies are byte-identical to the sources. There are no `application.yml` files anywhere in `lib/java`.

---

## 7. Deadman / heartbeat

**None.** No watchdog, no heartbeat, no deadman timer, no periodic ping in:
- `pathland-server-core` (grep for `heartbeat|deadman|keep-alive|ping` → 0 hits),
- either starter (0 hits),
- either demo (0 hits),
- the DOM client (`transport.ts`/`index.ts` — only reconnect-on-close with exponential backoff, `transport.ts:35-37, 114-133`).

The only "liveness" mechanisms are:
- Client reconnect + `META::RESYNC` on `onclose` (`transport.ts:94-108`, `index.ts:160-163`),
- Quarkus send-failure → close → client-reconnect (best-effort; §4 shows how it can silently fail),
- Nothing at all in the Spring path.

---

## Root-cause analysis (why deltas stop after a while)

The most probable culprit, in order:

1. **Spring starter: permanent silent stall after the first send failure.** Any transient write failure (network blip, proxy half-close, laptop sleep, tab throttling) makes `SpringConnection.send` throw; `PathlandSession.sendBatch` nulls the session connection but `closeConnection` is a **no-op because `SpringConnection` isn't `AutoCloseable`** (`SpringConnection.java:8`, `PathlandSession.java:160-168`). The Spring `WebSocketSession` stays open server-side, no close frame is sent, the client keeps `readyState === 1`, and **every subsequent delta is silently dropped at `endFrame`** (`PathlandSession.java:93-96`). No reconnect, no RESYNC — the exact "works initially, then events stop" symptom. `handleTransportError` only helps if the *container* notices an error, which it won't for a half-dead-but-never-closed socket.

2. **Quarkus starter: hung `sendBinary` stalls the serialized drain.** `QuarkusConnection.drain()` blocks all future sends once one in-flight subscription never completes or fails (`QuarkusConnection.java:45-66`). The client-side `transport.open` stays `true`, the server keeps emitting, but nothing is written. Close-on-failure (`failed = true` + `connection.close()`) only recovers if the close frame is actually deliverable — the close subscription swallows errors (line 64).

3. **No keepalive anywhere + a silent middlebox.** Because neither side pings, a proxy/LB/NAT idle timeout silently kills the TCP connection; the browser WebSocket never fires `onclose` (browsers don't keepalive WS), so the client never reconnects and the server (which can't tell) keeps or drops the session silently.

Concrete fixes the code itself points to: make `SpringConnection` (and `QuarkusConnection`) `AutoCloseable` so `PathlandSession.closeConnection` actually closes the adapter/session on failure; add a periodic ping (server `sendPing` / client `ws.ping()`); and have the client treat a missing expected delta (or a watchdog) as a dead connection rather than relying solely on `onclose`.

39: function eventBatch(command: number, a: number, b: number, c: number, opcodeFlags = 0): Uint8Array {
40:   const out = new Uint8Array(HEADER_SIZE + OPCODE_SIZE + 4);
41:   const view = new DataView(out.buffer);
42:   view.setUint32(0, MAGIC, true);
43:   view.setUint16(4, VERSION, true);
44:   view.setUint16(6, 0, true); // batch flags = guest -> host
45:   view.setUint32(8, 0, true); // frameCount
46:   view.setUint32(12, 1, true); // opcodeCount
47:   const pos = HEADER_SIZE;
48:   view.setUint8(pos, CAT_EVENT);
49:   view.setUint8(pos + 1, command);
50:   view.setUint16(pos + 2, opcodeFlags, true);
51:   view.setUint32(pos + 4, a, true);
52:   view.setUint32(pos + 8, b, true);
53:   view.setUint32(pos + 12, c, true);
54:   return out;
55: }

57: /** A META::RESYNC request (host → guest): ask the server for a full snapshot of the current tree. */
58: export function encodeResync(): Uint8Array {
59:   const out = new Uint8Array(HEADER_SIZE + OPCODE_SIZE + 4);
60:   const view = new DataView(out.buffer);
61:   view.setUint32(0, MAGIC, true);
62:   view.setUint16(4, VERSION, true);
63:   view.setUint16(6, 0x0001, true); // batch flags = HOST_TO_GUEST
64:   view.setUint32(8, 0, true); // frameCount
65:   view.setUint32(12, 1, true); // opcodeCount
66:   const pos = HEADER_SIZE;
67:   view.setUint8(pos, CAT_META);
68:   view.setUint8(pos + 1, CMD_RESYNC);
69:   view.setUint32(pos + 4, 0, true);
70:   view.setUint32(pos + 8, 0, true);
71:   view.setUint32(pos + 12, 0, true);
72:   return out;
73: }

96:   return eventBatch(CMD_KEY_DOWN, target, keyCode & 0xffff, modifiers & 0xff, repeat ? 0x0002 : 0);

143: /** A TEXT_CHANGED EVENT; the text rides in the batch's string section (B = relative offset). */
144: export function encodeTextChanged(target: number, text: string): Uint8Array {
145:   const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode(text);
146:   const out = new Uint8Array(HEADER_SIZE + OPCODE_SIZE + 4 + 4 + bytes.length);
147:   const view = new DataView(out.buffer);
148:   view.setUint32(0, MAGIC, true);
149:   view.setUint16(4, VERSION, true);
150:   view.setUint16(6, 0, true);
151:   view.setUint32(8, 0, true);
152:   view.setUint32(12, 1, true);
153:   const pos = HEADER_SIZE;
154:   view.setUint8(pos, CAT_EVENT);
155:   view.setUint8(pos + 1, CMD_TEXT_CHANGED);
156:   view.setUint32(pos + 4, target, true);
157:   view.setUint32(pos + 8, 0, true); // b = relative string offset (first entry)
158:   view.setUint32(pos + 12, 0, true);
159:   // string section: [stringsLen u32][entryLen u32][utf8…]
160:   const stringsAt = HEADER_SIZE + OPCODE_SIZE;
161:   view.setUint32(stringsAt, 4 + bytes.length, true);
162:   view.setUint32(stringsAt + 4, bytes.length, true);
163:   out.set(bytes, stringsAt + 8);
164:   return out;

194: // --- navigation (global, not node-keyed) ---
195: 
196: /** NAVIGATE to a URL (browser back/forward `popstate`, a deep link); the URL rides the string section. */
197: export function encodeNavigate(url: string): Uint8Array {
198:   const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode(url);
199:   const out = new Uint8Array(HEADER_SIZE + OPCODE_SIZE + 4 + 4 + bytes.length);
200:   const view = new DataView(out.buffer);
201:   view.setUint32(0, MAGIC, true);
202:   view.setUint16(4, VERSION, true);
203:   view.setUint16(6, 0, true);
204:   view.setUint32(8, 0, true);
205:   view.setUint32(12, 1, true);
206:   const pos = HEADER_SIZE;
207:   view.setUint8(pos, CAT_EVENT);
208:   view.setUint8(pos + 1, CMD_NAVIGATE);
209:   view.setUint16(pos + 2, FLAG_NAVIGATE_URL, true);
210:   view.setUint32(pos + 4, 0, true); // no target — global
211:   view.setUint32(pos + 8, 0, true); // b = relative string offset (first entry)
212:   view.setUint32(pos + 12, 0, true);
213:   const stringsAt = HEADER_SIZE + OPCODE_SIZE;
214:   view.setUint32(stringsAt, 4 + bytes.length, true);
215:   view.setUint32(stringsAt + 4, bytes.length, true);
216:   out.set(bytes, stringsAt + 8);
217:   return out;

220: /** NAVIGATE with no URL: a native back request (the app pops its own back-stack). */
221: export function encodeNavigateBack(): Uint8Array {
222:   return eventBatch(CMD_NAVIGATE, 0, 0, 0);
223: }

225: // --- environment (host → guest; META::ENVIRONMENT field family, spec/OPCODE.md) ---
226: 
227: /**
228:  * The platform's environment: viewport + initial route, as a batch of
229:  * `META::ENVIRONMENT` field opcodes (the route rides the batch's string section).
230:  * The DOM client sends this as its **first** message on connect and re-sends it to
231:  * **enrich** the environment after connect (e.g. a window resize re-emits the
232:  * viewport fields). The SSR host synthesizes the same message from the HTTP request.
233:  */
234: export function encodeEnvironment(width: number, height: number, route: string): Uint8Array {
235:   const routeBytes = new TextEncoder().encode(route);
236:   const out = new Uint8Array(HEADER_SIZE + 3 * OPCODE_SIZE + 4 + 4 + routeBytes.length);
237:   const view = new DataView(out.buffer);
238:   view.setUint32(0, MAGIC, true);
239:   view.setUint16(4, VERSION, true);
240:   view.setUint16(6, FLAG_HOST_TO_GUEST, true); // host (renderer) -> app
241:   view.setUint32(8, 0, true);
242:   view.setUint32(12, 3, true); // VIEWPORT_WIDTH, VIEWPORT_HEIGHT, ROUTE
243:   let pos = HEADER_SIZE;
244:   const field = (id: number, b: number) => {
245:     view.setUint8(pos, CAT_META);
246:     view.setUint8(pos + 1, CMD_ENVIRONMENT);
247:     view.setUint16(pos + 2, 0, true);
248:     view.setUint32(pos + 4, id, true);
249:     view.setUint32(pos + 8, b, true);
250:     view.setUint32(pos + 12, 0, true);
251:     pos += OPCODE_SIZE;
252:   };
253:   field(ENV_VIEWPORT_WIDTH, bitsFromF32(width));
254:   field(ENV_VIEWPORT_HEIGHT, bitsFromF32(height));
255:   field(ENV_ROUTE, 0); // route string at relative offset 0
256:   const stringsAt = pos;
257:   view.setUint32(stringsAt, 4 + routeBytes.length, true);
258:   view.setUint32(stringsAt + 4, routeBytes.length, true);
259:   out.set(routeBytes, stringsAt + 8);
260:   return out;
261: }

content.text:
## Reproduction — confirmed at https://pathland.onrender.com

I drove the live site with a **faithful protocol client** (same PLPL batches the DOM client sends: `META::ENVIRONMENT` handshake, `META::RESYNC`, pointer events, `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` every second like a playing client).

- Handshake + deltas work: RESYNC returns the full 394-op snapshot, play clicks return deltas, and during playback the server streams ~1 delta/sec.
- **The bug reproduces**: after ~3.9–4.5 minutes (233s / 269s in two runs), the server **silently stops sending** — the socket stays `open` (readyState 1), my continued messages get zero replies, no close, no error.
- **A fresh connection opened after the stall works perfectly** (streamed 158 deltas in 90s) → the app instance is healthy; the stall is **per-connection** — a connection silently dies and **neither side detects it**.

Root cause: the connection goes half-dead (most likely the Cloudflare↔Render upstream leg for that connection is dropped — Render's own docs warn about interrupted WS and recommend ping/pong + reconnect), and:
- **Client**: only reconnects on `onclose`/`onerror` (transport.ts:110–123), which never fire on a silently-stalled socket → no recovery, UI freezes.
- **Server (Quarkus)**: `QuarkusConnection.drain()` (QuarkusConnection.java:45–66) has **no timeout** — if a `sendBinary` Uni never completes, `sending` stays `true` forever, all future sends silently queue, `isOpen()` stays `true`, and `sendBatch` (PathlandSession.java:145–157) never sees a failure because Quarkus sends are async and never throw. A silent, permanent wedge.
- Server secondary gaps: `SpringConnection` isn't `AutoCloseable` so `closeConnection()` is a no-op (Spring send failure → silent drop, socket stays open); `DeltaBatcher.flush` runs the sender inside the lock (DeltaBatcher.java:97) so a blocking send stalls the actor/batcher.

(Note: my first probes appeared to "fail" but that was a bug in my probe — missing the trailing `stringsLen` field threw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` server-side. With correct frames everything above holds.)

## Proposed plan

**Phase 1 — Protocol heartbeat (spec-first)**. Add `META::PING = 0x04` (guest→host) and `META::PONG = 0x05` (host→guest): `spec/OPCODE.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `constants.rs`, regenerated `constants.ts` (`npm run regen`), `Commands.Meta` (Java).

**Phase 2 — Server: answer PING + surface send failures**
- Route `META::PING` → `META::PONG` in both sockets (Spring `PathlandSocket`, Quarkus `PathlandSocket`) via a `registry.pong(...)` → `PathlandSession.sendBatch(FrameCodec.encodePong())`.
- `QuarkusConnection`: add a send timeout (e.g. if the in-flight `sendBinary` doesn't complete in ~15s, mark `failed` and force-close the underlying connection) so the wedge becomes a recoverable close.
- `SpringConnection`: implement `AutoCloseable`/`close()` that closes the underlying `WebSocketSession`, so `PathlandSession.closeConnection` actually surfaces failures as a close.
- `DeltaBatcher.flush`: copy the pending batch under the lock, send **after** releasing it, so a blocking send can't stall the actor/batcher.

**Phase 3 — Client heartbeat + watchdog (the essential fix)**
- `transport.ts`: send `META::PING` every ~15s; track last received frame (any message, incl. PONG); if nothing arrives for ~45s, `ws.close()` → the **existing reconnect + RESYNC** path (transport.ts:94–108) self-heals.
- `applyMeta` already ignores unknown META commands safely (apply.ts:342–357), so PONG is a no-op on the DOM.

**Phase 4 — Tests, spec, status, verify**
- Rust: PING/PONG constants + conformance vectors. TS: `encodePing` bytes + watchdog unit tests. Java: `FrameCodec` PONG round-trip, session ping→pong, Quarkus send-timeout, batcher-outside-lock.
- Update all affected `status.md`; `cargo test`, `npm test`+typecheck, `mvn clean install`; re-run the live probe to confirm the client recovers after a stall.

Open questions for you:
1. Heartbeat cadence — 15s ping / 45s timeout reasonable? (Shorter = faster detection; longer = quieter.)
2. Also have the **server** send periodic protocol-level WS pings (browsers auto-pong, keeps the upstream leg warm + detects dead clients server-side)? Render's docs recommend this as the complementary side.

## Plan: WebSocket liveness — heartbeat + send-failure surfacing

### Phase 0 — Baseline (verify locally, optional)
Use the running `localhost:8080` to confirm current behavior with the probe (`ws://localhost:8080/_pathland/ws`), then re-validate after the fix before the live redeploy. The 4-min stall may not reproduce locally (it's most likely a Cloudflare↔Render upstream-leg drop), but the PONG replies, send-timeout, and heartbeat behavior can all be verified locally.

### Phase 1 — Protocol (spec-first)
Add **`META::PING = 0x04`** (guest→host) and **`META::PONG = 0x05`** (host→guest):
- `spec/OPCODE.md` (META command table), `spec/EVENTS.md` (heartbeat contract: client pings every 15 s, server answers PONG; server also sends WS protocol pings; client watchdog reconnects after 45 s of silence), `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` (add a PING/PONG golden vector if the meta commands are enumerated there).
- `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs` (`meta` module: `PING`, `PONG`).
- Regenerate `lib/typescript/src/constants.ts` via `npm run regen` (or `cargo run -p pathland-ts-codegen`).
- `lib/java/pathland-view/.../Commands.java` (`Commands.Meta`): `PING = 0x04`, `PONG = 0x05`.

### Phase 2 — Server (Quarkus) — surface send failures + answer PING + protocol pings
- **`QuarkusConnection.java`** (the core wedge):
  - **Send timeout**: arm a daemon timer when a `sendBinary` Uni is in flight; if it doesn't complete within **15 s**, mark `failed` and `connection.close()` (best-effort). Guard against late completion (a `with(...)` that fires after the timeout must not resume draining — check `failed` before clearing `sending`).
  - **Protocol pings**: a per-connection daemon `ScheduledExecutorService` sends `connection.sendPing(Buffer.buffer(4))` every **15 s** (client auto-pongs at the WS level); on failure → `failed` + close. Keeps the upstream leg warm and detects dead clients server-side. Same executor can arm the send-timeout.
- **`PathlandSocket.java`** (root) + **`MountedPathlandSocket.java`**: route `FrameCodec.isPing(message)` → `registry.pong(uiId())`.
- **`PathlandRegistry.java`**: `pong(uiId)` → `session(uiId, ...).pong()`.
- **`PathlandSession.java`**: `pong()` → `sendBatch(FrameCodec.encodePong())` (immediate reply).
- **`FrameCodec.java`**: `isPing(byte[])` + `encodePong()`.
- **`DeltaBatcher.java`**: move `sender.accept(...)` (line 97) **outside** the `synchronized` block — copy the merged batch under the lock, send after releasing — so a blocking send can never stall the actor/batcher.
- **Spring** (same `closeConnection` no-op bug; one small commit): make `SpringConnection` `AutoCloseable`/`close()` closing the underlying `WebSocketSession`, so `PathlandSession.closeConnection` surfaces send failures. (Not the live site, but the same latent silent-stall.)

### Phase 3 — Client (lib/typescript) — heartbeat + watchdog (the essential fix)
- `events.ts`: `encodePing()` — a `META::PING` batch, guest→host (36 bytes, mirrors `encodeResync`).
- `transport.ts`:
  - On `open`: `setInterval` → `send(encodePing())` every **15 s**; clear it on `close`/`stop`.
  - Watchdog: track `lastActivity` (reset in `onmessage` on **any** frame, incl. PONG); a 5 s checker forces `ws.close()` when `now - lastActivity > 45 s` → the **existing reconnect + RESYNC** path (transport.ts:94–108) self-heals.
  - Skip the check while `readyState !== OPEN`.
- `applyMeta` needs no change — it ignores unknown META commands (apply.ts:342–357), so a PONG batch is a DOM no-op.

### Phase 4 — Tests + status
- **Rust**: `PING`/`PONG` constants + conformance vector.
- **TS**: `encodePing` byte layout; heartbeat tests with a fake socket + fake timers — (a) ping every 15 s, (b) >45 s silence → `close()` → reconnect, (c) a PONG/message resets the watchdog (no reconnect), (d) an idle-but-ponging connection stays up.
- **Java**: `FrameCodec.encodePong`/`isPing` round-trip; `PathlandSession.pong` emits a PONG; `QuarkusConnection` send-timeout (fake `WebSocketConnection` whose Uni never completes → after 15 s `isOpen()` false + close called); DeltaBatcher sender-not-under-lock (a blocking sender doesn't stall `append`); Quarkus socket ping→pong routing.
- **status.md**: pathland-core, lib/typescript, pathland-view, pathland-server-core, pathland-quarkus-starter (+ demo-views note).

### Phase 5 — Verify + deploy
- `cargo test`, `npm test` + typecheck, `mvn clean install`.
- Local: `mvn quarkus:dev` → probe `ws://localhost:8080/_pathland/ws`: PONG replies to PING; connection survives the 4-min mark with the heartbeat.
- Live: probe `pathland.onrender.com` — after the fix the client should **recover within ~45 s** of a silent stall (reconnect + RESYNC), and deltas should stream continuously past the ~4-min stall point. This requires the **redeploy** after the user merges the branch.

Side benefit worth noting: the client's 15 s PING also keeps the connection non-idle through Cloudflare and — per Render's free-tier rules — counts as inbound WS traffic, preventing the 15-minute free-instance spin-down.

634: ## Transport
635: 
636: The opcode protocol is transport-agnostic. Two peer backends carry frames from
637: producer (guest engine) to consumer (host renderer):
638: 
639: | Backend | Scenario | Mechanism |
640: |---------|----------|-----------|
641: | Shared memory | Desktop / native (guest + host share linear memory) | The ring buffer + arena above; zero-copy |
642: | Network batch | SSR → browser (guest and host do **not** share memory) | Serialized batches of opcodes + arena delta |
643: 
644: The `Frame` type is the **transport seam**: a consumer (renderer) applies a
645: frame the same way whether it came from the shared-memory ring or a decoded
646: network batch.
647: 
648: ### Network batch format
649: 
650: ```
651: [u32 magic "PLPL"] [u16 version] [u16 flags] [u32 frameCount] [u32 opcodeCount]
652: [opcode × opcodeCount (16 B each)]
653: [u32 arenaDeltaLen] [arena delta bytes]
654: ```
655: 
656: - **magic / version**: `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`, little-endian on the wire) / `1`.
657:   A decoder MUST reject batches with a mismatched magic or version.
658: - **flags**: direction. `0x0000` = guest → host (tree/style). Bit `0x0001` =
659:   host → guest (raw-input events); host → guest batches carry their string
660:   payloads in the batch's string section.

662:   from multiple frames may coalesce into one batch; they remain in order).
663: - **arena delta**: the bytes appended to the bump arena since the previous
664:   batch. The consumer keeps a **mirrored arena** and appends each delta, so
665:   absolute `arenaRef` offsets stay valid — identical to shared memory.
666: - **META::RESET**: a batch containing a reset opcode clears the consumer's
667:   mirrored arena before appending (offsets restart at 0).

Yes — and the existing issue is **#58 "Web client: heartbeat + frameCount gap detection"** (OPEN). This plan implements its heartbeat half; the frameCount-gap half stays P3 on the issue.

## Should we spec it? Yes — but explicitly scoped to the network transport.

The wire encoding crosses three implementations (TS client, Java server, and the Rust `pathland-core-transport` batch codec), and the project's rule is spec-first with golden vectors for exactly this cross-language agreement. If it's not spec'd, the encodings drift. But the **scope** must be drawn so it can't leak into the ring path.

### The scoping is structural, not just prose
PING/PONG ride only in **PLPL batches** (`META` opcodes in the network batch format). The shared-memory ring backend never serializes batches — `pathland-core`, `pathland-core-capi`, `pathland-view-native`, and the GTK renderer don't touch the batch format. So the heartbeat is network-only **by construction**, and its presence in the shared META command table is no more dangerous than the existing precedent: `RESYNC`/`ENVIRONMENT` are already META commands that only the network/SSR layer uses — the ring engine never emits them.

### What goes in the spec

content.text:
The relationship: heartbeat and frameCount-gap detection are **two orthogonal failure detectors** that #58 bundles. They answer different questions, recover differently, and neither can substitute for the other.

## Heartbeat = transport liveness
- **Question:** *Is the connection alive at all?* Catches a silent stall — half-open socket, proxy (Cloudflare↔Render) dropping the leg, server send-path wedge. The defining case: **no frames arrive**, so there's no gap to detect.
- **Recovery:** the connection can't be trusted to deliver an in-band request, so it's the heavy path — `ws.close()` → existing reconnect → env + `META::RESYNC` (transport.ts:94–108).

## frameCount gap = stream integrity on a live pipe
- **Question:** *Did I receive every delta on a connection I trust?* Catches **partial loss** — a dropped WS message, a coalescing edge — where PONGs still flow (pipe is alive) but a frame was missed, so the client's DOM tree silently diverges from the server.
- **Recovery:** lightweight and in-band — a `META::RESYNC` request **over the existing connection** (no reconnect needed). Coalescing-aware: compare the previous batch's `frameCount + opcodeCount` to the new batch's `frameCount`; a jump means missed frames → RESYNC.

## Why neither subsumes the other
- A silent stall produces **no batches** → no gap → only the heartbeat sees it.
- A dropped mid-stream frame is **not** a liveness failure → PONGs keep coming → only the gap detector sees it.

## Current state of frameCount (the gap half's prerequisite)
- **Rust** `pathland-core-transport`: `Batch` carries and encodes a real `frame_count` (batch.rs:31,89).
- **Java server**: `Frame` has no counter, and `FrameCodec.encodeFrame` hardcodes `frameCount = 0` (FrameCodec.java:40); `FrameOpcodeSink` has `framesProduced` but it never reaches the wire. So the live server sends 0 in every batch.
- **TS client**: parses `frameCount` (plpl.ts:46) but never uses it (transport.ts:4–5 calls gap handling "P3").

So gap detection can't work until the server stamps a real per-session counter through `Frame` → `DeltaBatcher` (which coalesces and must carry the first frame's counter) → `encodeFrame`.

## How they compose
Both live in the client's `handleMessage` and share the RESYNC seam — the heartbeat's watchdog is the natural home for "no frames for 45 s → reconnect", and the gap check slots into the same handler ("frameCount jumped → RESYNC"). They're additive, not overlapping.

## Recommendation
Keep them as **separate, sequential efforts** (as planned): land the **heartbeat now** — it fixes the reproduced live bug and is fully self-contained. Keep **frameCount gap detection as the P3 half of #58**, with a prerequisite note added to the issue (Java must stamp real frameCount). When the gap half lands, the heartbeat + watchdog already give it a hook and the RESYNC recovery path is shared. #58 stays open until both halves are in.

Want me to add that prerequisite note to #58 as part of this plan, or leave the issue untouched?
add note...  And then go with ping pong if you suggest we have that still

Yes — I still recommend the app-level **META PING/PONG**, and I'll add the #58 prerequisite note as the first execution step (plan mode forbids changes now).

**Why ping/pong is needed** (not just server-side WS pings): browsers expose **no** `ws.ping()` and **no** pong event — the WebSocket API only lets the *server* send protocol pings, which the browser auto-answers invisibly. So protocol pings keep the connection warm and let the server detect a dead client, but they give the **client** no signal to detect a silently-wedged server. The only way the client can probe liveness and observe a reply is an app-level message pair over the batch channel → `META::PING`/`META::PONG`. That's what closes the reproduced bug (client recovers ~45 s after a silent stall).

**Confirmed approach:** both halves, as you approved:
- Client sends `META::PING` every 15 s; watchdog closes + reconnects if no frame for 45 s.
- Server answers `META::PONG`; `QuarkusConnection` send-timeout (15 s) + 15 s WS protocol pings (server-side detection + keepalive).

**Updated plan — Step 0 first:**
1. Comment on **#58** recording the frameCount prerequisite: *"Heartbeat half (PING/PONG + client watchdog) is implemented in the WS reliability work; the frameCount-gap half remains P3. Prerequisite: the Java server currently hardcodes `frameCount=0` in `FrameCodec.encodeFrame` (Frame.java has no counter; DeltaBatcher coalesces frames). Gap detection needs a real per-session monotonic counter plumbed through `Frame` → `DeltaBatcher` (first-frame counter) → `encodeFrame`, then the client checks `prev.frameCount + prev.opcodeCount vs new.frameCount` and requests RESYNC on a jump."*
2. Then implement per the plan: **Phase 1** spec+constants (PING=0x04, PONG=0x05, OPCODE.md META table + Transport heartbeat subsection, CONFORMANCE vector), **Phase 2** server (Quarkus), **Phase 3** client, **Phase 4** tests/status, **Phase 5** local + live verification.

Everything's decided — approve the plan (exit plan mode) and I'll start with the #58 note, then the spec + constants.
Yes. But 45 seconds is just too long for recovering..

Agreed — let's tighten it. The recovery bound is `watchdog + one ping interval` (the last PONG can be up to a full interval before the stall), so a 45 s watchdog actually means up to ~60 s.

**Proposed values:**
- Client ping: **every 5 s** (~36-byte batch, trivial; also counts as inbound WS traffic for Render free spin-down)
- Client watchdog: **15 s** of no frame of any kind → force close + reconnect. Recovery ≈ **15–20 s** worst case (typically ~15.5 s, since the first reconnect backoff is only 500 ms)
- Server send-timeout (`QuarkusConnection` hung `sendBinary`): **10 s** → mark failed + close (when the wedge is server-side, the client sees the close and reconnects in ~1 s without waiting for the watchdog)
- Server WS protocol pings: **15 s** keepalive (unchanged — this is detection/keepalive, not recovery latency)

All four are named constants so they're trivial to retune later. 15 s of total silence (3 missed ping rounds) is decisive enough that spurious reconnects shouldn't be a concern.

Everything else stays as planned: Step 0 = #58 prerequisite comment, Phase 1 = spec+constants (PING 0x04 / PONG 0x05), Phase 2 = Quarkus server, Phase 3 = client heartbeat+watchdog, Phase 4 = tests/status, Phase 5 = local + live verification.

Good to go on 5 s ping / 15 s watchdog / 10 s server send-timeout? Approve the plan and I'll start executing.

### Batching policy

The producer buffers opcodes and flushes a batch when **either** threshold is
reached (first trigger wins):

- **Time**: the interval since the first buffered opcode elapses (default **4 ms**).
- **Size**: the accumulated batch reaches a network-frame size (default **1400 bytes**).

Both thresholds are configurable; a producer MAY flush eagerly (e.g. on the
first frame after connection).

### Transport heartbeat

The **network batch backend** (a WebSocket / streamed connection) can fail
silently: a proxy or load balancer may drop the connection without a close
frame, or the peer's send path may wedge, leaving the socket "open" while
nothing is delivered. Neither side can detect this from the batch stream alone.
The heartbeat is the transport-liveness mechanism for this backend:

- **Probe**: the guest (client) sends a `META::PING` batch at a fixed cadence
  (default **every 5 s**). `A/B/C = 0`, no string section.
- **Reply**: the host (server) MUST answer each `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
  batch as promptly as its send path allows.
- **Liveness**: a peer's *liveness* is any received batch — deltas, `PONG`, or
  anything else. A guest that receives no batch for **more than two probe
  intervals** SHOULD treat the connection as dead: close it and reconnect (the
  reconnect flow already re-syncs via `META::RESYNC`).
- **Host-side detection**: a host MAY additionally send WebSocket-protocol-level
  ping frames (browsers auto-answer) to detect a dead client and keep
  middleboxes from timing the connection out; a host whose send fails (or a
  probe that is never answered) SHOULD close the connection so the client
  reconnects instead of stalling.
- **Scope**: the heartbeat is **transport liveness only, NOT app state**. A
  `META::PING`/`META::PONG` batch MUST NOT be routed into the application — it
  never touches the retained tree, signals, or events. The **shared-memory ring
  backend MUST NOT use it**: ring peers are co-located and their liveness is the
  host process's concern, so the ring never carries, expects, or relays
  `META::PING`/`META::PONG`.

205: ## Directions
206: 
207: - `TREE` / `PARAMETER` are **guest → host** (application → renderer).
208: - `EVENT` is **host → guest** (renderer → application): raw pointer/keyboard
209:   inputs with a host-resolved `targetId`. A conforming EVENT encoder/decoder
210:   MUST reproduce vectors 8–12 and 21–22 exactly.
211: - `META` is both directions.
212: 
213: ## Frame Conformance
214: 
215: A complete frame is: delta opcodes written into consecutive ring slots, then a
216: `frameCount` increment in the header block. Ring slot `i` occupies bytes
217: `[ringOffset + i*16, ringOffset + i*16 + 16)`.
218: 
219: The header block layout and ring semantics are defined in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#linear-memory-layout).
220: 
221: The host → guest event ring shares the same 16-byte slot format and lives at
222: `eventRingOffset` (header `0x2A`), with `eventReadCursor` (0x36, guest-owned)
223: and `eventWriteCursor` (0x3A, host-owned). A host writing `EVENT:POINTER_UP`
224: into the event ring must reproduce the exact vector-11 bytes in the slot at
225: `eventWriteCursor`, then advance `eventWriteCursor`; the guest advances
226: `eventReadCursor` after draining.
227: 
228: String-bearing events (`TEXT_CHANGED`, `NAVIGATE` with the `NAVIGATE_URL`
229: flag) resolve their text from the host → guest **event arena** (header
230: `eventArenaOffset` 0x40 / `eventArenaCursor` 0x48, host-owned, shared memory)
231: or the batch's string section (network) — the same dual absolute/relative
232: convention as `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT`. See OPCODE.md's
233: [event arena](./OPCODE.md#event-arena-host--guest) section.

238: [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#transport)). A conforming batch encoder/decoder MUST
239: reproduce the following bytes exactly.

244: delta is the self-describing entry for `"Hi"`: `[02 00 00 00][48 69]`.

- **`QuarkusConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketConnection` to `PathlandConnection`.
  Sends are **serialized** (one `sendBinary` subscription in flight, the rest queued),
  and a **send failure closes the connection** so the session drops it and the DOM
  client reconnects + `META::RESYNC` (recoverable) instead of silently stalling on an
  "open" socket that never delivers (the remote seekbar symptom). **Send timeout**: a
  `sendBinary` that neither completes nor fails within 10 s (a half-dead connection /
  a dropped proxy upstream leg) is marked failed and closed — a hung send would
  otherwise wedge the serialized drain forever. **Keep-alive pings**: the connection
  sends a WS-protocol ping every 15 s (browsers auto-pong) to keep the connection warm
  through middleboxes and detect a dead client; `close()` stops the keep-alive
  scheduler (the sockets' `@OnClose` calls it).
- **Heartbeat** — both sockets route a client `META::PING` to `registry.pong`
  (spec/OPCODE.md §Transport heartbeat): the server answers with a `META::PONG` batch,
  giving the DOM client its liveness signal.

Phase 2: Quarkus server (send-timeout, pings, PONG route, batcher-outside-lock)

content.text:
Done. Committed as `b31e274e` on **`feat/ws-heartbeat`** (based on `main` @ `371b4dbd`, which already has the media-echo merge #118).

## What landed
**Protocol (spec-first)** — `META::PING = 0x04` (guest→host) / `META::PONG = 0x05` (host→guest), **network-batch-transport-only**: spec/OPCODE.md META table + new "Transport heartbeat" section, CONFORMANCE vectors 13a/13b/16a, `constants.rs` → regen `constants.ts`, Java `Commands.Meta`, Rust golden vectors. The shared-memory ring path never emits/expects/relays them (same precedent as RESYNC/ENVIRONMENT).

**Client (`lib/typescript`)** — sends PING every **5 s**; watchdog forces `close()` → reconnect + RESYNC when no server frame of any kind arrives for **15 s** (recovery ≤ ~20 s worst case). PINGs also count as inbound WS traffic, keeping Render-free instances alive.

**Server (Quarkus)** — root + mounted sockets route PING → `registry.pong` → `META::PONG`. `QuarkusConnection`: **10 s send-timeout** (a hung `sendBinary` → failed + close, un-wedging the silent serialized-drain stall) + **15 s WS-protocol keep-alive pings** (dead-client detection); sockets close the connection on `@OnClose`. **Spring** parity: PING routing + `SpringConnection` is now `AutoCloseable` so send failures surface as a close. `DeltaBatcher` sends **outside the lock** so a blocking send can't stall the actor/batcher.

**#58** — prerequisite note added for the frameCount-gap half.

## Verified
- cargo: 30 suites green (incl. new PING/PONG vectors).
- TS: typecheck + **186 tests** (new: ping cadence, no-activity reconnect, PONG resets watchdog, `encodePing` byte-exact vs vector 16a).
- Java: full `mvn clean install` green — incl. `QuarkusConnectionTest` (timeout/drain/ping), `FrameCodecTest`, session+registry pong, batcher-outside-lock.
- **End-to-end local**: ran the freshly-built demo jar on :8081 → PING answered with a PONG in 12 ms; RESYNC returned the 394-op snapshot.

## Next step (yours)
Merge `feat/ws-heartbeat` → Render redeploys the Quarkus demo → I'll re-probe the live site to confirm the client now recovers (~15 s after a stall) instead of freezing.

## Diagnosis: the server is fine — the served **client bundle** is stale

- **Server (8080): verified working.** My probe got a PONG (`cat=4 cmd=5`) 7 ms after a PING. The `PING → registry.pong → PONG` path is live on your instance.
- **The browser client never sends PINGs** because `/_pathland/dom-renderer.js` it loads is the **old bundle** (44,584 B, no heartbeat). The rebuilt `dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` (47,982 B, has the heartbeat) was built at 22:13 but **never copied into the demos** — both committed copies (`quarkus-demo` `META-INF/resources`, `spring-demo` `static`) still have zero heartbeat markers.
- **Why I missed it:** I ran `npm run build` but not `copy-to-demos`. And CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:136–139`) runs only `typecheck`/`test`/`build` — it does **not** copy to demos, so even a deploy from the repo would serve the stale bundle.

## Plan (on approval)

1. `cd lib/typescript && npm run build:all` — rebuild `dist` and copy it into both demos (`quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/_pathland/`, `spring-demo/src/main/resources/static/_pathland/`).
2. Verify both copied bundles contain the heartbeat (`grep "no server frame"` > 0).
3. Commit the two bundle copies (required — otherwise the redeploy serves the old client too).
4. Kill the stray 8081 jar process left from my earlier verification.
5. You restart the IntelliJ `quarkus:run` (it serves from `target/classes`; a restart is needed to pick up the new resource), then hard-reload the browser → PINGs every 5 s, PONGs back, watchdog armed.

## Optional follow-up
Add `npm run copy-to-demos` to CI after `build`, so the demos' bundles never silently drift from `dist` again (this bug is exactly that drift).

2. Committed `dff1c3cb` (the two bundle copies).
3. Repackaged the quarkus demo — the app jar now embeds the 47,982 B heartbeat bundle.
4. Started the rebuilt app on 8080 (your previous instance had gone down).

- Served `/_pathland/dom-renderer.js` now contains the heartbeat client code.
- PING → **PONG in 179 ms**.

Should ping/pong control frames be 0x9 / 0xA?

No — those are two different layers, and 0x04/0x05 are correct for Pathland's META opcodes.

**The 0x9/0xA are RFC 6455 WebSocket *control-frame* opcodes** (Ping = 0x9, Pong = 0xA) — part of the transport stack itself. That's exactly what the server's `sendPing` in `QuarkusConnection` emits (via Vert.x), and what the browser auto-answers with a Pong, invisibly. We never define or number those; they're fixed by the standard and handled by the WS layer.

**Our `META::PING`/`META::PONG` (0x04/0x05) are Pathland 16-byte opcodes riding inside PLPL batches** — an *application-level* heartbeat on the batch channel, in Pathland's own `META` command space (RESET 0x01, ENVIRONMENT 0x02, RESYNC 0x03, PING 0x04, PONG 0x05). They exist because a browser client can't send WS pings (`ws.ping()` doesn't exist) and never sees pong events, so it can't probe server liveness with control frames — it needs a message it sends and gets a reply to.

The two coexist and are complementary:
- **Server → browser** WS Ping/Pong (0x9/0xA): keep-alive + dead-client detection, automatic on the browser side.
- **Client → server → client** `META::PING`/`PONG` (0x04/0x05): the client's liveness probe + watchdog, which is what actually recovers a silently-stalled connection.

Renumbering Pathland's opcodes to 0x9/0xA would imply a wire-level relationship that doesn't exist (META 0x04/0x05 live in a 16-byte opcode, not a WS frame header) and would break the sequential META allocation. The spec's scoping note already distinguishes them — "PING/PONG ... network batch transport only" vs. "a host MAY additionally send WebSocket-protocol-level ping frames."

So: keep 0x04/0x05. If you'd like, I can add a one-line clarification to `spec/OPCODE.md §Transport heartbeat` spelling out that the META opcodes are distinct from the RFC 6455 control frames — want that?

Another ai had these findings: roblemet
WebSocket-forbindelsen er ustabil.
Nogle gange fungerer den fint i lang tid. Andre gange mister browseren forbindelsen meget hurtigt, ofte inden for ca. 15 sekunder.
Det virker derfor ikke som en simpel Render idle-timeout. Jeg vil gerne finde den faktiske root cause i Pathlands WebSocket-/concurrency-implementation.
Observation
Klienten har en heartbeat/watchdog-mekanisme omkring:
* META::PING hvert ca. 5 sekund
* watchdog omkring 15 sekunder uden modtaget servertrafik
* reconnect hvis watchdog udløses
Der findes desuden server-side WebSocket protocol ping/keepalive omkring 15 sekunder.
Jeg er derfor bekymret for, at heartbeat-mekanismen måske reagerer på en intern blokering i Pathland og fejlagtigt konkluderer, at WebSocket-forbindelsen er død.
Foreløbige fund
Jeg har analyseret koden og har især bemærket følgende:
1. PathlandRegistry bruger en single-threaded actor
PathlandRegistry ser ud til at serialisere application events via én ExecutorService / actor-thread.
Det betyder, at ting som:
* WebSocket events
* PING/PONG handling
* state updates
* rendering/delta generation
* browser events
kan ende med at vente på samme executor.
Undersøg derfor meget grundigt, om en langsom eller blokeret operation på actor-threaden kan forhindre heartbeat/PONG i at blive behandlet hurtigt nok.
2. Application heartbeat ser ud til at gå gennem application actor
Den relevante flow ser omtrent ud til at være:
Browser → META::PING → WebSocket handler → PathlandRegistry → actor queue → PathlandSession → WebSocket connection → META::PONG
Det virker potentielt problematisk.
Et heartbeat burde principielt ikke være afhængigt af application state eller en event-loop/actor, der også håndterer tungere arbejde.
Undersøg om META::PONG bør håndteres direkte på transportlaget:
Browser → WebSocket handler → immediate PONG
uden at gå gennem PathlandRegistry.
3. QuarkusConnection har et fælles sending-flag
Der ser ud til at være en AtomicBoolean sending, som bruges til at serialisere WebSocket sends.
Undersøg især interaktionen mellem:
* sendBinary()
* sendProtocolPing()
* sending
* SEND_TIMEOUT_MILLIS
* PING_INTERVAL_MILLIS
Jeg har bemærket, at en protocol ping tilsyneladende kan blive droppet, hvis en anden send allerede ejer sending.
Undersøg om dette kan skabe race conditions, starvation eller falske timeout-situationer.
4. Send timeout og heartbeat timeout ligger meget tæt
De relevante værdier ser ud til at være cirka:
* client PING: 5 sekunder
* client watchdog: 15 sekunder
* server protocol ping: 15 sekunder
* server send timeout: 10 sekunder
Det giver kun få sekunders margin.
Jeg vil dog IKKE acceptere "ændr bare 15 sekunder til 30 sekunder" som en løsning.
Det kan gøre systemet mere tolerant, men det forklarer ikke, hvorfor en ellers sund WebSocket mister forbindelse.
