content.text:
Fixed. The play/pause icon failing to change was a **client-side self-match bug** in the lazy resolver (not the emitter or server):

## Root cause
`setIcon` rewrote the element's `data-pathland-icon` to the new name **before** scanning for an embedded glyph — and that scan includes the element itself. So on the play→pause delta, the button svg suddenly "matched" its own new attr and pasted back its **old play glyph** → the icon never changed (no fetch, no error). A freshly created in-document icon also self-copied empty content.

## Fix (`lib/typescript/src/icons.ts`)
`setIcon` now **resolves before mutating** — the memo/embedded-glyph lookup runs against the truthful pre-mutation DOM (the button still advertises `play`), so `pause` falls through to the fallback + lazy fetch of `/_pathland/icons/pause.svg`. SSR-parity attr assignment stays on the success paths.

## Regression coverage (+3 tests, 206 total pass)
- `icons.test.ts`: **same-element toggle on a hydrated svg** (play→pause→play), asserting it never pastes its own glyph; fresh in-document icon never left blank.
- `apply.test.ts`: a real `PROP_ICON_NAME=pause` **delta over a hydrated play button** — the live WS path.

## Verified
- Both demos serve glyphs: Spring (`/_pathland/icons/play|pause.svg` → 200, `image/svg+xml`, `immutable`) and Quarkus (global **and** mounted `/app2` base — RESTEasy falls through, no shadowing).
- `npm test` 206 pass, golden `--check` current, bundle rebuilt + re-copied to both demos (51,283 B).

**One thing on your side:** something (PID 74889) still occupies port **8080** — if that's your Spring demo, it's running the **old jar/bundle** (with the bug), which is also exactly the "stale running server" trap from before. Restart it from the freshly built `pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar`, then hard-refresh the browser. The changes are uncommitted — say the word if you want them committed.

Great.. It works..  One thing I am wondering is that when I click play, it loads and show the pause icon. When I click play again it load and shows the play icon. Why does it load the play icon. Is it not embedded from the start?

Great question — your intuition is right, and the reason it fetches is a one-time gap in my memoization. Here's what happens:

## Why "play" loads after "pause"

Play **is** embedded from the start — but only as **DOM content**, never entered into the client's JS memo:

1. SSR shows the button svg `data-pathland-icon="play"` + the play `<path>` inline.
2. Click → delta `pause` → `setIcon`: pause is in no cache, appears nowhere in the DOM → **fetch pause.svg** (memoized after).
3. Click → delta `play` → `setIcon`: `cache.get("play")` is **a miss** (play was never *fetched* — its embedded copy was DOM-only), and the only play svg was the button, which now advertises `pause` → no embedded play remains → **fetch play.svg**.

So the embedded seed is "single-use": the instant the element flips to pause, play stops being discoverable anywhere. Each side loads exactly once (then both are memoized), but the return trip to play can be made instant.

## Fix — harvest embedded glyphs into the memo on first miss

Add a small `harvestEmbedded()` in `icons.ts`: on a `setIcon` miss, scan the document's `svg.pathland-icon[data-pathland-icon]` once and write each glyph into `cache` (skipping empty content), then re-check. Same behaviour as today, plus:

- t0: button = play (embedded).
- t1 → pause: miss → **harvest saves play's glyph into the cache** → pause still absent → fetch pause (once).
- t2 → play: **cache hit → instant, no fetch.**
- t3 → pause: cache hit → instant.

The CSS "SSR is the preload" idea becomes explicit in the memo instead of a per-query scan. Static pages that never toggle icons pay nothing (harvest only runs on a miss).

## Change set
- `lib/typescript/src/icons.ts`: add `harvestEmbedded()`; call it in the `setIcon` miss path before falling back/fetching (re-check memo after).
- `test/icons.test.ts`: update the in-place toggle test to assert the **return trip is instant** (no fallback, no second fetch); add a case proving a superseded glyph is reused.
- `npm test` (206+), `npm run build:all` (rebundle + copy), golden check.
- `lib/typescript/status.md`: note the embedded-seed memo.

content.text:
Full picture now. The ~1/sec cadence is the same contract in three places:

**Web** (`apply.ts:1222`): `timeupdate` handler throttles to `|currentTime − lastReported| ≥ 1` (~1 report/s; browser `timeupdate` is only ~4 Hz anyway, so 30 Hz needs a real sampler).
**GTK** (`render-gtk/lib.rs`): worker polls every 250 ms → drains every 250 ms → `should_report_time` gates on `≥ 1.0 s` advance (two 250 ms + a 1 s gate = ~1/s).
**Spec** (`EVENTS.md:280`): "Reported … advances ~1 second (at most ~1/s)".

## Plan — 30 reports/s (~every 33 ms of progress)

**Web (`apply.ts`)**
- Replace the throttled `timeupdate` with a **33 ms `setInterval` sampler** (guarded by `!media.paused`; reports when `currentTime − lastReported ≥ 1/30`). Store the timer id on `mediaState.reportTimer`.
- **Clear the interval** in `CMD_DELETE_NODE` (apply.ts:442) so a removed media node stops sampling.
- Keep `ended` + the seek echo-guard (`> 0.25` at :1274 — still valid at 30 Hz: a delayed echo sits well inside 0.25 s of the latest report).

**GTK (`render-gtk/src/lib.rs`)**

What is the performance penalty?

Negligible — this is one of the cheapest places to spend 30 Hz. Breakdown:

**Wire cost (the only real cost)**
- Each `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` is **one 16-byte EVENT opcode** (id + `seconds` f32).
- At 30 Hz: **≈ 480 B/s** up (report) + if the app echoes into the seek bar, ~480 B/s of `SET_PROPERTY` back. Total **~1 KB/s round-trip per playing audio** — noise next to the media stream itself (a 128 kB/s MP3 is 100× that).

**Web sampler**
- A `setInterval` at 33 ms with a trivial handler: one float compare + `performance.now()` check + occasionally an event encode + WS send. ~30 wakeups/s doing **microsecond-scale** work — far under 0.1% of a core. Buried under the browser's animation/render loop.

**GTK sampler**
- Worker loop `recv_timeout` 250→33 ms: 30 wakeups/s instead of 4, with a **`query_position` on playbin** per wake (~µs-level; GStreamer cheaply reports running time). Main-thread drain timer at 33 ms is 30 no-op timeout callbacks/s. Still sub-1% of one core. Scales linearly per playing node (demo has one).

**Two watch-items (not blockers)**
1. **App-side amplification**: every report flushes the app's position signal → the emitter re-emits only the bound nodes (~1 more opcode each) 30×/s. Fine-grained emission keeps this trivial; only *persisted* state or heavy computed chains would amortize badly — the demo neither persists position nor computes much per report.
2. **Background throttling**: browsers cap background-tab timers to ≥1 s, and GTK timers throttle on an occluded window — so the 30 Hz is best-effort when the app is visible/focused, which is exactly when it matters.

So the penalty is effectively **zero measurable CPU**, ~1 KB/s of WS traffic, and the only "cost" is the app side getting 30 updates/s to reconcile (which is the point).

Here's what I found and the design space, again — now pegged to **parent-container size** (not viewport), which is exactly SwiftUI's layout-container model.

## The model

`ViewThatFits`/`SizeThatFits` is a **layout container, not a structural container** — a key distinction from `Conditional`:
- **All candidates are always children of the node** (the wire/tree describes the full alternative set; no app-side pick, no structural reconcile — so it works identically in the Java and Rust DSLs and adds nothing to the emitter).
- **The renderer picks**, based on the size *it* was allocated by its parent (GTK `size_allocate`; the CSS/JS container size on web). The pick is a pure function of (tree, allocated size) — renderer-owned layout output, consistent with "renders may retain their layout tree; never app state."
- A **new `PARAMETER` property set** tells the renderer how to pick; a **new component id** (`0x17`, free in the reserved 0x17–0x1A layout range) is the container.

## Two candidate designs

| | **A — `ViewThatFits` (SwiftUI-faithful)** | **B — `SizeThatFits` / width-query** |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | first child whose **measured ideal size** fits the container | first child whose declared **width threshold** (e.g. `minWidth`) the container **meets** (a band) |
| Web | needs candidates' ideal sizes → JS `ResizeObserver` + measure (flicker risk) *or* app-supplied ideal hints + CSS `@container` | **pure CSS `@container (min-width/max-width)`** — native layout, zero JS, correct at SSR first paint |
| GTK | `gtk_widget_measure` each child in allocator (native, cheap) | numeric band compare in the allocator (cheaper) |
| Cross-renderer | **diverges**: fonts/platform metrics differ → same px can pick differently on GTK vs web | **deterministic**: app-declared thresholds vs container px → identical picks everywhere |
| Perf | O(candidates) structural change only; measurement on change/resize | O(candidates) structural change only; **zero** steady-state, browser re-evaluates `@container` on its own resize |

**Perf verdict**: **B is the clearest win** — the web path is a pure CSS container-query band (each candidate = one `@container (min-width: tᵢ) and (max-width: tᵢ₊₁)` rule; sorted ascending, last band unbounded — natively exclusive, no measurement, no JS, no round-trip, no reflow feedback), and GTK is a one-time numeric compare in the allocator. A is fully possible but pays measurement + a cross-renderer consistency cost.

Both satisfy "what's possible across renderers": web (SSR + DOM), GTK, and any future renderer get the same contract — only the picker differs, and the spec defines the algorithm (candidate order = priority; last candidate = fallback when nothing fits).

## Proposed plan (recommended: B, bolted to the existing drafts)

1. **Spec-first**: allocate the container (`VIEW_THAT_FITS` 0x17 / name TBD) in `PRIMITIVES.md` + `LAYOUT.md`; define `FIT_AXIS` (0x1016) + reuse the **already-drafted** per-candidate `MIN_WIDTH`/`IDEAL_WIDTH`/`MAX_WIDTH` (0x334/336/338) as the threshold hints; specify the container is **size-taking** (never hugs — a fitted container in a HUG context is degenerate); hidden candidates are `display:none`/`visible=false` (inert: no hit-test/ARIA); document renderer-owned pick = layout output, not state. DSL.md rows + CONFORMANCE vectors.
2. **Core**: `component_type` + `property_id` + constants test.
3. **Render-html (SSR)**: emit `<div … class="pathland-ftf" style="container-type:inline-size">` + a generated document `<style>` with the sorted candidate `@container` bands; mirror in the DOM client's `elements.ts` shell + `apply.ts` `FIT_*` handling (no measurement JS).
4. **Render-gtk**: allocator picks the band, `set_visible` on the winner.
5. **DSLs**: Java `ViewThatFits/SizeThatFits.of(axis, candidates …)` (candidate `oof…` / `.fitting(minWidth)`) + a Rust `pathland-view` counterpart (~a retained container with the same props).
6. **Golden** fixtures (SSR shows only the winning candidate visible + correct CSS), `ssr-conformance`, TS/GTK/Java tests, `status.md` updates.

## Decisions I need from you

Before I finalize the plan in detail:

Locked: **B — `SizeThatFits` (width-query on parent-container size)**, both DSLs. Here is the final plan.

## Semantics (spec-defined)
- `SIZE_THAT_FITS` container (component **0x17**): a size-taking layout container — it stretches to the size its parent proposes (it never hugs; a fitted container in a HUG context is degenerate and documented as such).
- Each candidate child carries **`MIN_WIDTH`** (reuses the already-drafted `0x334`, F32 = logical points). No threshold ⇒ 0.
- **Pick rule**: sort candidates ascending by `MIN_WIDTH` (stable — ties keep child order); render the candidate with the **largest threshold the container width meets**; the lowest-threshold candidate is the always-applicable fallback. Before first measure (e.g. initial SSR), render the narrowest candidate — the browser immediately re-applies container queries at layout.
- **Losers are inert**: `display:none` (web) / `set_visible(false)` + non-focusable (GTK) — no hit-testing, no ARIA, no `EVENT` routing.
- Renderer picks = layout output (pure function of tree + allocated width), not app state. Spec documents the algorithm so GTK and web agree when inputs agree.

## Web: pure CSS, zero JS
- SSR emits `<div data-pathland-id class="pathland-ftf" style="container-type:inline-size;container-name:pathland-ftf">` around the candidates; a generated per-document `<style>` block appends **exclusive `@container` bands**: candidate *i* → `@container pathland-ftf (min-width: tᵢ) and (max-width: tᵢ₊₁−1px)` (last band unbounded). Children query their nearest named container ancestor — which is their own parent. Native layout resolves the winner; correct at **SSR first paint**; re-evaluates for free on any resize. No measurement, no `ResizeObserver`, no round-trip.
- DOM client mirrors the shell + `MIN_WIDTH` data on candidates (`elements.ts` + property handling); no measurement logic in `apply.ts`.

## GTK: allocator compare
- In the container's `size-allocate`, compute `max{MIN_WIDTHᵢ ≤ width}` → `set_visible(true)` that child, all others hidden (inert). Reads stored child properties; O(candidates) per allocate, cached by GTK's own allocation stability.

## Work items
1. **Spec-first**: `OPCODE.md` (component 0x17, MIN_WIDTH alias to 0x334 + its per-candidate semantics), `PRIMITIVES.md` + `LAYOUT.md` (container sizing contract, pick algorithm, hidden-candidate rule), `CONFORMANCE.md` vectors, `DSL.md` surface rows (Java + Rust columns).
2. **Core**: `constants::component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS = 0x17` (no new property needed — MIN_WIDTH already exists); constants test; Java `Components`/`Properties` mirror; `npm run regen`(constants.ts).
3. **DSLs (parity)**: Java `SizeThatFits.of(Fit...)` with `Fit.of(view, minWidth)` / `Fit.any(view)` (minWidth 0), plus a Rust `pathland-view` `SizeThatFits`/`Fit` equivalent emitting the same properties. No emitter change (all candidates are plain children; no structural scope needed).
4. **render-html (SSR)**: container shell + head `@container` band styles; golden `sizethatfits` fixture (visible winner + hidden losers + CSS); `ssr-conformance` + a TS test (band exclusivity).
5. **render-gtk**: allocator band pick + visibility; unit test for the pick rule.
6. **Java/Rust DSL tests** (emitter produces 0x17 + per-candidate MIN_WIDTH); `status.md` for core/view/render-html/render-gtk/java-view/typescript.
7. **Verify**: cargo per-crate, `npm test`, golden `--check`, `mvn install`, `npm run build:all` + repack demos.

**Perf**: zero steady-state cost on both renderers; only the O(candidates) band pick on structural change (or re-alloc/resize); no socket traffic, no measurement, no feedback loop. **Cross-renderer**: identical picks (app-declared thresholds in logical points vs container width).

One note: this opt's **"largest threshold that fits wins"** (threshold-driven). If you want SwiftUI's strict *child-order = preference, first that fits wins* instead, it's the same machinery with the sort reversed — say so and I'll fold it into the spec.

If only the selected child is transmitted, the **app must decide before emission**, which means the renderer feeds the container's width back to the app (a report), the app selects, and the emitter transmits exactly one child via a structural slot. The constraint reshapes the design cleanly — and the necessary machinery already exists. Here's the revised plan.

## Revised model: app-side selection, only the pick transmitted

- `SizeThatFits` becomes a **structural container** (like `Conditional`): the **candidates live only in the DSL** (their `MIN_WIDTH` thresholds never ride the wire). The app selects using the **container's reported width** and the emitter transmits **exactly one child** through the slot — `TREE` deltas swap it when the width band changes; an unchanged selection emits **zero opcodes**.
- The renderer's job is reduced to: (1) size the container node to its parent's proposal, (2) when its allocated width changes, **report it** (a new host→guest event). Selection, comparison, and emission are all app/engine-side — "applications are Smart."
- **This is the `Conditional` precedent, proven**: `Emitter.reconcileSlot` already re-runs on any signal read inside `structuralContent.get()` and diffs/reconciles (identical recompute → zero opcodes). `SizeThatFits` reuses that verbatim, with the width signal as the selector. `RenderResult` already returns routed-input registries (taps/text/value/media) — a `size` sink slots into the same pattern.

## New protocol surface (minimal)
- `component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS = 0x17` (slot container; FILL-sized so it has a measurable width).
- `property_id::MEASURE` (0x1016): opt-in "report this node's allocated size" so only fitted containers are measured (no blanket reporting).
- **`event::SIZE_CHANGED` (0x13)**: host→guest, `{targetId, width (B f32), height (C f32)}`.

## Across renderers — yes, uniformly
- **Web**: SSR emits `<div data-pathland-id class="pathland-ftf" data-pathland-measure style="width:100%;align-self:stretch">` + the selected child. The DOM client attaches a **`ResizeObserver`** (rAF-throttled) and sends `SizeChanged` on hydration + on resizes. No candidate measurement; unselected candidates are never mounted.
- **GTK**: the container is a FILL-sized widget; in `size-allocate`, when the width changes ≥1, emit `Event::SizeChanged` through the existing event ring/sink.

Yes — that's a genuine improvement, and it's compatible with everything you've pinned down. Here's the refined design.

## The hybrid: renderer measures, app transmits

**What the renderer receives**: the fit **query** — the sorted candidate **threshold table** (`[720, 480, 0]`) as a LIST property on the container — plus the **currently selected child** (only ever one child on the wire, as you required).

**What the renderer does**: it already knows its own allocated width from its layout pass (no extra measurement work). It compares that width against the threshold table locally and **only emits one event — `FIT_CHANGED{target, index}` — once after first measure and then whenever the derived fit index actually changes** (a band crossing).

**What the app does**: nothing on ordinary resizes (no inbox traffic); on `FIT_CHANGED` it swaps the DSL-local candidate via the existing structural reconcile — which emits **zero opcodes if the new index maps to the same view**.

## Why it beats reporting the raw size
- **Wire**: resize events (which can be dozens per drag-resize) **never reach the app** — the table is transmitted once, and only discrete fit transitions round-trip. Strictly less traffic than `SIZE_CHANGED` at full width resolution.
- **Latency**: detection is immediate/local; the round-trip happens only when the new subtree must actually be materialized.
- **Constraint honored**: candidate *views* never ride the wire — only the app's single selected child does; the "extra" is the tiny, set-once threshold list.
- **Determinism (unchanged)**: same rule ("largest threshold ≤ measured width", logical points) + same numbers → identical picks on every renderer; candidates remain app-owned.
- **Smaller protocol than the raw-size plan**: we can **drop the `MEASURE` property entirely** (the container is identified by its component type + query present). Renderers need only a local ResizeObserver (web, to *detect* changes, never report size) / a compare in `size-allocate` (GTK).

## New protocol surface (delta)
- `component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS = 0x17` (FILL-sized slot; unselected children never transmitted).
- `property_id::FIT_QUERY = 0x1016`, value type **`LIST`** — arena-backed `[u32 count][f32 × count]` sorted ascending (stable; equal thresholds → lower index wins). A new `value_type::LIST` ID (0x09) is a clean spec addition (mirrors the token-path arena convention); a STRING-packed layout is the fallback if you'd rather not add a value type.
- `event::FIT_CHANGED = 0x13`: `{target, index (f32/U32)}` — emitted on first measure + on transition only.

## Model
`SizeThatFits` is a **structural slot container** (reuses the `Conditional`/`reconcileSlot` machinery). The app holds the candidates DSL-local (each with a `minWidth`), transmits the **threshold table** (`FIT_QUERY`) plus the **currently-selected child only**; the renderer measures its own allocated width, computes the fit **locally**, and emits `FIT_CHANGED{index}` only on the first measure and on **transitions** — never a size stream. - **`component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS = 0x17`** (layout/container gap), FILL-sized (stretches to parent proposal; never hugs — documented).
- **`value_type::LIST = 0x09`** — arena-backed `[u32 count][f32 × count]` (mirrors the token-path arena convention).
- **`property_id::FIT_QUERY = 0x1016`** (LIST): sorted-ascending thresholds; equal → lower index wins (stable).
- **`event::FIT_CHANGED = 0x13`** (host→guest, `{target, index}`): emitted once after first measure, then only on derived-index change.
- **Fit rule (spec)**: show `max{i : thresholds[i] ≤ width}` (fallback index 0); renderer measures in logical points → identical picks on every renderer.

input.newString:
### LazyHStack — `LAZY_HSTACK` 0x1C

Virtualized horizontal stack. **Allocation is identical to `HStack`**; only
realization is windowed.

### SizeThatFits — `SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17

A **fit slot**: it shows **one child at a time — the currently selected
candidate — so only that child is ever transmitted**. The app owns the
candidates (their views never ride the wire); it transmits the **fit query**
(`FIT_QUERY`, LIST — the candidates' `minWidth` thresholds, ascending) plus the
selected child. The renderer measures its **own allocated width** (the slot is
size-taking — it stretches to its parent's proposal, never hugs, so it always
has a well-defined width) and selects the fit **locally**:

> **Fit rule** — the selected index is `max{ i : thresholds[i] ≤ measured
> width }` (threshold 0 candidate always qualifies — the fallback); equal
> thresholds pick the **lower index**; before the first measure the app renders
> the threshold-0 candidate (index 0). The measurement is in **logical points**,
> so the pick is identical on every renderer given the same slot width.

The renderer reports its selection back with **`FIT_CHANGED`** ([EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md))
— emitted **once after the first measure, and then only when the derived fit
index changes** (a band crossing). It never streams the raw size. The app reacts
by swapping the slot's child (a `TREE` delta pair); a selection that maps to the
already-shown view re-emits **zero** opcodes.

Semantics:
- **Properties**: `FIT_QUERY` (`0x1032`, LIST).
- **Events**: `FIT_CHANGED` (`0x13`, host → guest) — reported fit index.
- **Children**: at most one (the current selection); candidate views live
  app-side.
- **Renderer statelessness**: the measured width and derived index are layout
  output, not retained application state.

### Containers

Stacks, scroll, and other containers lay their children out inside; a Fixed box
constrains them (scroll for `SCROLLVIEW`, otherwise overflow is visible unless
`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it).

### Size that fits (`SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17)

A fit slot is **size-taking on both axes**: it stretches to its parent's
proposal (`FILL` semantics — never hugs), because its **allocated width is the
unit of fitting**. It holds at most one (selected) child, laid out normally
inside the box. The renderer measures its allocated width and derives the fit
index (threshold rule in [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md#size-that-fits)). No
content-based measurement of candidates is ever done or transmitted — the query
thresholds are app-declared, so the pick is a pure function of
`(thresholds, allocated width)`.

24: /// offset).
25: #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
26: pub enum Event {
27:     /// Pointer button pressed at a viewport-relative point.
28:     PointerDown {
29:         target: u32,
30:         x: f32,
31:         y: f32,
32:         secondary: bool,
33:     },
34:     /// Pointer moved; optionally entered/left the node (hover).
35:     PointerMove {
36:         target: u32,
37:         x: f32,
38:         y: f32,
39:         hovering: bool,
40:         leaving: bool,
41:     },
42:     /// Pointer button released at a viewport-relative point.
43:     PointerUp {
44:         target: u32,
45:         x: f32,
46:         y: f32,
47:         secondary: bool,
48:     },
49:     /// Key pressed (possibly an auto-repeat).
50:     KeyDown {
51:         target: u32,
52:         key_code: u16,
53:         modifiers: u8,
54:         repeat: bool,
55:     },
56:     /// Key released.
57:     KeyUp {
58:         target: u32,
59:         key_code: u16,
60:         modifiers: u8,
61:     },
62:     /// A control's value changed (host → guest). The renderer resolves the
63:     /// semantic value (e.g. a slider thumb dragged along its track) and reports
64:     /// it here; the guest/app writes it into its bound state.
65:     ValueChanged {
66:         target: u32,
67:         value: f32,
68:     },
69:     /// A text field's value changed (host → guest). The new text is resolved
70:     /// from the batch's string section (see the doc comment on this enum).
71:     TextChanged {
72:         target: u32,
73:         value: String,
74:     },
75:     /// A node gained/lost focus (host → guest). Draft command 0x08.
76:     FocusChanged { target: u32, focused: bool },
77:     /// An editing session began/ended (host → guest). Draft command 0x09.
78:     EditingChanged { target: u32, editing: bool },
79:     /// The user committed a field (host → guest). Draft command 0x0A.
80:     Submit { target: u32 },
81:     /// A scroll container's offset changed (host → guest). Draft command 0x0B.
82:     Scroll {
83:         target: u32,
84:         offset_x: f32,
85:         offset_y: f32,
86:     },
87:     /// Raw wheel/trackpad deltas (host → guest). Draft command 0x0C.
88:     Wheel {
89:         target: u32,
90:         delta_x: f32,
91:         delta_y: f32,
92:     },
93:     /// A `DATE_PICKER`'s value changed (host → guest). Draft command 0x0D;
94:     /// `days` is I32 (pre-1970 negative), `millis` is millis of day.
95:     DateChanged {
96:         target: u32,
97:         days: i32,
98:         millis: u32,
99:     },
100:     /// A global navigation request (host → guest). Draft command 0x0E; never
101:     /// node-keyed. `url: Some(...)` carries the destination URL the platform
102:     /// navigated to (browser `popstate`/back/forward/deep-link), resolved from
103:     /// the string section / event arena; `url: None` is a native back request.
104:     Navigate { url: Option<String> },
105:     /// A bound `AUDIO`/`VIDEO` node's playback state changed (host → guest).
106:     /// Draft command 0x0F; reported only when `PLAYBACK_STATE` is bound.
107:     MediaPlayStateChanged { target: u32, playing: bool },
108:     /// A bound media node's current playback position (host → guest). Draft
109:     /// command 0x10; `seconds` is the position in seconds (f32), reported while
110:     /// playing. An app-initiated seek (`MEDIA_POSITION` change) is not echoed.
111:     MediaTimeUpdated { target: u32, seconds: f32 },
112:     /// A bound media node reached the end of its media (host → guest). Draft
113:     /// command 0x11.
114:     MediaEnded { target: u32 },
115:     /// A bound media node's volume changed (host → guest). Draft command 0x12;
116:     /// `volume` is in the range 0..1 (f32).
117:     MediaVolumeChanged { target: u32, volume: f32 },
118: }

120: impl Event {
121:     /// Encode this event as a 16-byte opcode.
122:     ///
123:     /// `TextChanged` and `Navigate` with a URL cannot be fully encoded here —
124:     /// their strings live in the batch's string section / event arena — so this
125:     /// emits the opcode with a zero `B` offset; the batch-aware
126:     /// `encode_events`/`decode_events` pair in `pathland-core-transport` writes
127:     /// the string and its real offset.
128:     pub fn encode(&self) -> Opcode {
129:         match self {
130:             Event::PointerDown {
131:                 target,
132:                 x,
133:                 y,
134:                 secondary,
135:             } => Opcode::new(
136:                 category::EVENT,
137:                 crate::event::POINTER_DOWN,
138:                 flag_for(*secondary, false, false),
139:                 *target,
140:                 x.to_bits(),
141:                 y.to_bits(),
142:             ),
143:             Event::PointerMove {
144:                 target,
145:                 x,
146:                 y,
147:                 hovering,
148:                 leaving,
149:             } => Opcode::new(
150:                 category::EVENT,
151:                 crate::event::POINTER_MOVE,
152:                 flag_for(false, *hovering, *leaving),
153:                 *target,
154:                 x.to_bits(),
155:                 y.to_bits(),
156:             ),
157:             Event::PointerUp {
158:                 target,
159:                 x,
160:                 y,
161:                 secondary,
162:             } => Opcode::new(
163:                 category::EVENT,
164:                 crate::event::POINTER_UP,
165:                 flag_for(*secondary, false, false),
166:                 *target,
167:                 x.to_bits(),
168:                 y.to_bits(),
169:             ),
170:             Event::KeyDown {
171:                 target,
172:                 key_code,
173:                 modifiers,
174:                 repeat,
175:             } => Opcode::new(
176:                 category::EVENT,
177:                 crate::event::KEY_DOWN,
178:                 if *repeat { flag::KEY_REPEAT } else { 0 },
179:                 *target,
180:                 *key_code as u32,
181:                 *modifiers as u32,
182:             ),
183:             Event::KeyUp {
184:                 target,
185:                 key_code,
186:                 modifiers,
187:             } => Opcode::new(
188:                 category::EVENT,
189:                 crate::event::KEY_UP,
190:                 0,
191:                 *target,
192:                 *key_code as u32,
193:                 *modifiers as u32,
194:             ),
195:             Event::ValueChanged { target, value } => Opcode::new(
196:                 category::EVENT,
197:                 crate::event::VALUE_CHANGED,
198:                 0,
199:                 *target,
200:                 value.to_bits(),
201:                 0,
202:             ),
203:             Event::TextChanged { target, .. } => Opcode::new(
204:                 category::EVENT,
205:                 crate::event::TEXT_CHANGED,
206:                 0,
207:                 *target,
208:                 0,
209:                 0,
210:             ),
211:             Event::FocusChanged { target, focused } => Opcode::new(
212:                 category::EVENT,
213:                 crate::event::FOCUS_CHANGED,
214:                 0,
215:                 *target,
216:                 u32::from(*focused),
217:                 0,
218:             ),
219:             Event::EditingChanged { target, editing } => Opcode::new(
220:                 category::EVENT,
221:                 crate::event::EDITING_CHANGED,
222:                 0,
223:                 *target,
224:                 u32::from(*editing),
225:                 0,
226:             ),
227:             Event::Submit { target } => Opcode::new(
228:                 category::EVENT,
229:                 crate::event::SUBMIT,
230:                 0,
231:                 *target,
232:                 0,
233:                 0,
234:             ),
235:             Event::Scroll {
236:                 target,
237:                 offset_x,
238:                 offset_y,
239:             } => Opcode::new(
240:                 category::EVENT,
241:                 crate::event::SCROLL,
242:                 0,
243:                 *target,
244:                 offset_x.to_bits(),
245:                 offset_y.to_bits(),
246:             ),
247:             Event::Wheel {
248:                 target,
249:                 delta_x,
250:                 delta_y,
251:             } => Opcode::new(
252:                 category::EVENT,
253:                 crate::event::WHEEL,
254:                 0,
255:                 *target,
256:                 delta_x.to_bits(),
257:                 delta_y.to_bits(),
258:             ),
259:             Event::DateChanged {
260:                 target,
261:                 days,
262:                 millis,
263:             } => Opcode::new(
264:                 category::EVENT,
265:                 crate::event::DATE_CHANGED,
266:                 0,
267:                 *target,
268:                 *days as u32,
269:                 *millis,
270:             ),
271:             Event::Navigate { url } => Opcode::new(
272:                 category::EVENT,
273:                 crate::event::NAVIGATE,
274:                 if url.is_some() { flag::NAVIGATE_URL } else { 0 },
275:                 0,
276:                 0,
277:                 0,
278:             ),
279:             Event::MediaPlayStateChanged { target, playing } => Opcode::new(
280:                 category::EVENT,
281:                 crate::event::MEDIA_PLAY_STATE_CHANGED,
282:                 0,
283:                 *target,
284:                 u32::from(*playing),
285:                 0,
286:             ),
287:             Event::MediaTimeUpdated { target, seconds } => Opcode::new(
288:                 category::EVENT,
289:                 crate::event::MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED,
290:                 0,
291:                 *target,
292:                 seconds.to_bits(),
293:                 0,
294:             ),
295:             Event::MediaEnded { target } => Opcode::new(
296:                 category::EVENT,
297:                 crate::event::MEDIA_ENDED,
298:                 0,
299:                 *target,
300:                 0,
301:                 0,
302:             ),
303:             Event::MediaVolumeChanged { target, volume } => Opcode::new(
304:                 category::EVENT,
305:                 crate::event::MEDIA_VOLUME_CHANGED,
306:                 0,
307:                 *target,
308:                 volume.to_bits(),
309:                 0,
310:             ),
311:         }
312:     }
313: }

315: /// Build a pointer-opcode flags word from the pointer/hover bits.
316: #[inline]
317: fn flag_for(secondary: bool, hovering: bool, leaving: bool) -> u16 {
318:     let mut flags = 0u16;
319:     if secondary {
320:         flags |= flag::POINTER_SECONDARY;
321:     }
322:     if hovering {
323:         flags |= flag::HOVER_ENTER;
324:     }
325:     if leaving {
326:         flags |= flag::HOVER_LEAVE;
327:     }
328:     flags
329: }

331: /// Error decoding a raw-input event from an opcode.
332: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
333: pub enum EventError {
334:     /// The opcode is not an `EVENT` category opcode.
335:     NotAnEvent,
336:     /// The opcode is an EVENT category opcode but an unknown command.
337:     UnknownCommand,
338:     /// The opcode is `TEXT_CHANGED`, which needs the batch's string section to
339:     /// resolve its text; decode it with `pathland-core-transport::decode_events`
340:     /// instead of a bare opcode.
341:     NeedsStringSection,
342: }
343: 
344: impl TryFrom<Opcode> for Event {
345:     type Error = EventError;
346: 
347:     fn try_from(op: Opcode) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
348:         if op.category() != category::EVENT {
349:             return Err(EventError::NotAnEvent);
350:         }
351:         let flags = op.flags();
352:         match op.command() {
353:             crate::event::POINTER_DOWN => Ok(Event::PointerDown {
354:                 target: op.a(),
355:                 x: op.b_f32(),
356:                 y: op.c_f32(),
357:                 secondary: flags & flag::POINTER_SECONDARY != 0,
358:             }),
359:             crate::event::POINTER_MOVE => Ok(Event::PointerMove {
360:                 target: op.a(),
361:                 x: op.b_f32(),
362:                 y: op.c_f32(),
363:                 hovering: flags & flag::HOVER_ENTER != 0,
364:                 leaving: flags & flag::HOVER_LEAVE != 0,
365:             }),
366:             crate::event::POINTER_UP => Ok(Event::PointerUp {
367:                 target: op.a(),
368:                 x: op.b_f32(),
369:                 y: op.c_f32(),
370:                 secondary: flags & flag::POINTER_SECONDARY != 0,
371:             }),
372:             crate::event::KEY_DOWN => Ok(Event::KeyDown {
373:                 target: op.a(),
374:                 key_code: op.b() as u16,
375:                 modifiers: op.c() as u8,
376:                 repeat: flags & flag::KEY_REPEAT != 0,
377:             }),
378:             crate::event::KEY_UP => Ok(Event::KeyUp {
379:                 target: op.a(),
380:                 key_code: op.b() as u16,
381:                 modifiers: op.c() as u8,
382:             }),
383:             crate::event::VALUE_CHANGED => Ok(Event::ValueChanged {
384:                 target: op.a(),
385:                 value: op.b_f32(),
386:             }),
387:             crate::event::FOCUS_CHANGED => Ok(Event::FocusChanged {
388:                 target: op.a(),
389:                 focused: op.b() != 0,
390:             }),
391:             crate::event::EDITING_CHANGED => Ok(Event::EditingChanged {
392:                 target: op.a(),
393:                 editing: op.b() != 0,
394:             }),
395:             crate::event::SUBMIT => Ok(Event::Submit { target: op.a() }),
396:             crate::event::SCROLL => Ok(Event::Scroll {
397:                 target: op.a(),
398:                 offset_x: op.b_f32(),
399:                 offset_y: op.c_f32(),
400:             }),
401:             crate::event::WHEEL => Ok(Event::Wheel {
402:                 target: op.a(),
403:                 delta_x: op.b_f32(),
404:                 delta_y: op.c_f32(),
405:             }),
406:             crate::event::DATE_CHANGED => Ok(Event::DateChanged {
407:                 target: op.a(),
408:                 days: op.b() as i32,
409:                 millis: op.c(),
410:             }),
411:             crate::event::TEXT_CHANGED => Err(EventError::NeedsStringSection),
412:             crate::event::NAVIGATE => {
413:                 if flags & flag::NAVIGATE_URL != 0 {
414:                     Err(EventError::NeedsStringSection)
415:                 } else {
416:                     Ok(Event::Navigate { url: None })
417:                 }
418:             }
419:             crate::event::MEDIA_PLAY_STATE_CHANGED => Ok(Event::MediaPlayStateChanged {
420:                 target: op.a(),
421:                 playing: op.b() != 0,
422:             }),
423:             crate::event::MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED => Ok(Event::MediaTimeUpdated {
424:                 target: op.a(),
425:                 seconds: op.b_f32(),
426:             }),
427:             crate::event::MEDIA_ENDED => Ok(Event::MediaEnded { target: op.a() }),
428:             crate::event::MEDIA_VOLUME_CHANGED => Ok(Event::MediaVolumeChanged {
429:                 target: op.a(),
430:                 volume: op.b_f32(),
431:             }),
432:             _ => Err(EventError::UnknownCommand),
433:         }
434:     }
435: }

437: /// Decode an event opcode for the **shared-memory path**, resolving
438: /// `TEXT_CHANGED` text and `NAVIGATE` URLs from the host → guest event arena
439: /// (`B` is an absolute offset into that region). Non-string events decode as
440: /// usual.
441: ///
442: /// Returns `None` for non-event opcodes, unknown commands, or string events
443: /// whose offset cannot be resolved (invalid or out of range).
444: pub fn decode_event(op: &Opcode, event_arena: &[u8]) -> Option<Event> {
445:     if op.category() != category::EVENT {
446:         return None;
447:     }
448:     if op.command() == crate::event::TEXT_CHANGED {
449:         let text = crate::arena::get_str(event_arena, op.b()).ok()?;
450:         return Some(Event::TextChanged {
451:             target: op.a(),
452:             value: text.to_string(),
453:         });
454:     }
455:     if op.command() == crate::event::NAVIGATE && op.flags() & flag::NAVIGATE_URL != 0 {
456:         let url = crate::arena::get_str(event_arena, op.b()).ok()?;
457:         return Some(Event::Navigate {
458:             url: Some(url.to_string()),
459:         });
460:     }
461:     Event::try_from(*op).ok()
462: }

content.text:
The `SizeThatFits` feature is implemented on **`feat/size-that-fits`** (7 commits) across the full vertical slice, all green.

## What landed
- **Protocol (spec-first)**: `SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17, `FIT_QUERY` 0x1039 (new **LIST** value type 0x09 — arena `[u32 count][f32×count]`), `FIT_CHANGED` 0x13; fit rule + sizing contract in `LAYOUT.md`/`PRIMITIVES.md`; conformance vectors (LIST property + event).
- **Core**: constants, `Event::FitChanged`, and `pathland_core::fit::fit_index` — the one spec'd pick algorithm every renderer shares.
- **Wire**: TS constants regen, TS `readList` + `encodeFittedChanged`; Java `Components`/`Properties`/`ValueTypes`/`Commands` + `FrameCodec` decode.
- **Java DSL**: `SizeThatFits.of(Fit...)` — a structural slot that transmits **only the selected child**; `FIT_QUERY` emitted, `FIT_CHANGED` routed into the slot via `RenderResult.fitInputs` → structural reconcile swaps the child (zero opcodes on no-op). FrameOpcodeSink + RingOpcodeSink write LIST.
- **Server**: `InputDispatcher` routes `FIT_CHANGED` into the fit sink.
- **Web**: SSR renders the fit slot with `data-pathland-fit`; the DOM client derives the fit locally on a per-slot `ResizeObserver` and reports only transitions (teardown on delete).
- **Golden/status**: `sizethatfits` fixture pinned in `ssr-conformance`; 219 TS + 117 Java + all cargo tests green; demo bundles rebuilt/copied.

## Deliberately deferred (recorded in `status.md` gaps)
- **Rust DSL/engine**: `Component::SizeThatFits` + LIST emission + a static Fit surface (needs careful engine arena work).
- **GTK renderer**: allocator width-compare → `set_visible`/`FIT_CHANGED`.

If you want, I'll continue with the Rust DSL + GTK next — they were the two remaining scope items from the plan.

Good question — the difficulty isn't the *concept* (the web version of this took ten minutes with `ResizeObserver`), it's that **GTK4 gives you no size-change notification at all**, and the crate's design revolves around stock widgets.

## Why GTK makes this hard

**1. GTK4 removed the size-change signal.** GTK3 had `GtkWidget::size-allocate` (a signal you could `connect`); **GTK4 deleted it** — sizes are imposed top-down by the parent during layout, and there is deliberately no "my allocation changed" callback. I just confirmed `gtk4-0.9.7` (the pinned version) exposes `WidgetExt::size_allocate` (a method to *force* an allocation) but **no `connect_size_allocate`**. That's the immediate compile error you saw — the hook I'd naturally reach for doesn't exist.

**2. The GTK4 way to observe size is heavyweight.** To react to a size change in GTK4 you must either
- **subclass `GtkWidget`** with a `glib::ObjectSubclass` and override `allocate` (a `GObject` class registration + struct boilerplate the whole renderer currently avoids — it only ever builds stock `GtkBox`/`GtkLabel`/… widgets), or
- **poll on the frame clock** via `WidgetExt::add_tick_callback(...)` — a per-vsync callback (60/s) where you read `widget.allocation().width()` and compare. This exists (`gtk4-0.9.7/src/widget.rs:16`) and needs no subclassing, just a per-slot one-shot attach + teardown.

**3. The renderer has no "attach-once observation" seam for lifetime-bound callbacks.** `apply_frame → sync()` rebuilds/updates widgets every frame, and the only analogous machinery is the `attached_listeners`/`attached_sessions` idempotency guards (signal connections pruned on `DELETE_NODE`). A frame-clock observer needs the same pattern: a `fit_states: HashMap<nodeId, Rc<RefCell<FitState>>>` with thresholds + last index, pruned on delete — the `sync_fit` design I already sketched fits, but the *observer source* has to be the tick callback, not a signal.

**4. Headless testability.** `pathland-render-gtk`'s tests are pure logic (no display), so the actual widget-allocation observation can't be exercised here — only the upstream pieces (`pathland_core::fit::fit_index`, the GTK host's `list_csv` LIST decode) are unit-testable.

## The fix (small, bounded)
Swap the planned observer source from the nonexistent signal to the **frame-clock tick callback**:
- In `sync_fit`, attach `widget.add_tick_callback(...)` once per fit slot (guarded by the `fit_states` entry), keeping the returned `glib::SourceId` for teardown on `DELETE_NODE` (like the media `seek_timer` pattern).
- The callback (only running while the slot exists, ~60/s) reads `allocation().width()` as f32, runs `fit_index(&thresholds, width)`, and emits `Event::FitChanged` only when it changes — the same transition-only contract as the web side.
- Keep the existing `widget_kind`/`is_container`/`stack_layout` additions so the slot renders as a fill `GtkBox`, plus the host.rs `LIST → CSV` decode (done) and a unit test for `list_csv`.

Cost per fitted slot: one idle frame tick (cheap; the demo has at most a handful). On a static window it's a no-op compare; on resize it emits only on band crossings — matching the web's behavior.

Here's an honest complexity read of the GTK renderer.

## Overall scope — a full embedded native renderer, ~5.2k LOC

| File | LOC | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `lib.rs` | 3,348 | All widget creation/mapping, incremental sync, **media pipeline**, **libadwaita navigation**, styling/CSS, input wiring, GTK run loop |
| `layout.rs` | 962 | Native layout mapping (stacks/grids/zstacks/frames/spacers, fill-propagation) |
| `host.rs` | 600 | Frame → `HostNode` decode (tree, props, strings, tokens) |
| `capi.rs` | 160 | `pathland_gtk_*` C ABI for Java/JNA hosts |
| `tokens.rs` | 137 | Token defaults + GTK-native theme enrichment |

It's roughly the same *size* as the HTML SSR renderer (`render-html` lib.rs ~3.6k), but the per-line complexity is far higher because it's **stateful widget code**, not string formatting.

## Where the real complexity lives (the hard 20%)

1. **GStreamer media pipeline** (~`media_worker_loop`/`MediaPlayer`, 200+ lines): a dedicated worker thread owning a `playbin`, an mpsc control channel, a main-thread report router, seek **debounce + echo guards**, 30 Hz position polling. This is genuinely intricate (threaded GStreamer lifecycle).
2. **libadwaita navigation mirroring** (NavigationView/Page stacks, back-stack depth bookkeeping, `popped`→`NAVIGATE`): reconciling an external back-stack with a widget's internal page stack without double-pushing.
3. **Native styling**: building GTK **CSS** from opcodes, Pango typography/font-description mapping, token resolution plus GTK-theme-color enrichment (`gtk_defaults` overlaying the app tokens).
4. **Incremental widget sync**: `sync()`/`get_or_create`/`update`/`sync_container` reconciling a retained widget map, children order/positions, composite control bodies, grid cells — the DOM-client logic re-implemented against GTK idioms.
5. **Input routing**: per-node gesture controllers (pointer/hover/scroll/key/focus) gated by `EVENT_LISTENERS`, drag in-flight suppression.

## Where `SizeThatFits` fits (it's a *small corner*, not the hard parts)

The feature itself touches none of the hard subsystems. My earlier implementation pass already landed the easy, safe pieces:

- `widget_kind`/`is_container`/`stack_layout` — the slot becomes a fill `GtkBox` (single child) ✓
- `host.rs` LIST → CSV decode (`list_csv`) for `FIT_QUERY` ✓
- the `sync_fit` design + `FitState` thresholds/last-index map with delete-pruning ✓

The only blocker left is the **observer source**, because GTK4 has no size-change signal. Two options, both small:

- **A. Frame-clock tick (`add_tick_callback`) — recommended.** Attach once per fit slot (idempotency-guarded by the `fit_states` entry, like `attached_listeners`), keep the `glib::SourceId` for teardown. Each vsync (~60/s, only while the slot exists) read `allocation().width()`, run `pathland_core::fit::fit_index`, emit `Event::FitChanged` only on band crossings. ~40 lines, no architecture change, mirrors the web's transition-only contract.
- **B. Custom widget subclass (`glib::ObjectSubclass`, override `allocate`).** "Proper" GTK4 idiom but drags in GObject subclassing boilerplate the crate deliberately avoids — not worth it for a one-child observ-as-you-go slot.

Headless testability: the pure pieces (core `fit_index`, `list_csv`, a `fit_state` change-detection helper) are unit-testable; the actual frame-clock emission can't run without a display, same as every other widget behavior here.

So: **the GTK renderer as a whole is one of the largest, most intricate crates in the workspace, but the SizeThatFits increment rides only the style/layout seams and is a ~40-line contained change (Option A).** Want me to go ahead with Option A on `feat/size-that-fits`?

content.text:
Confirmed against the pinned bindings — and the answer to "doesn't GTK4 have built-in visual reactivity?" is: **it has three distinct reactive mechanisms, and none of them is "pick a child by your own allocated size."** A `ViewThatFits`/`SizeThatFits` container does not exist in GTK4, by design.

## The three built-in reactivity models in GTK4

**1. Size negotiation / demand-driven relayout** (`gtk4-0.9.7/src/auto/widget.rs`): a widget declares its natural sizes via the `GtkSizeRequest` vfuncs (`measure`/`size_allocate`); to *request* a relayout it calls `queue_resize()`/`queue_allocate()` and GTK re-runs the negotiation. So "I changed what I want" is reactive — but the *imposed* size flows **down from the parent**, and there is **no callback/signal when a widget's allocation changes** (the GTK3 `size-allocate` signal was removed; that's the exact blocker we hit). A widget only learns its size by overriding `allocate` (subclass) or sampling it (tick callback).

**2. Constraint-based adaptive layout** — `GtkConstraintLayout` (`constraint_layout.rs`): Auto-Layout-style relational/target constraints (`width ≥ 320`, `width = parent·0.5`, preferred-range). This is GTK's "responsive *parameters*" primitive — the analog of CSS media queries on size — but it adapts *one* view's geometry; it never selects among **alternative subtrees**.

**3. App-/user-driven page switching** — `GtkStack` + `gtk_stack_set_visible_child_name`, and libadwaita's `AdwViewStack`/`AdwViewSwitcher` (`view_stack.rs`): show one child out of many, but selection is **programmatic (the app) or user-driven (a switcher)** — never automatic by available width.

Plus the "readability" extras: **`AdwClamp`/`AdwClampScrollable`** (`clamp.rs`) constrain content to a preferred max-width (a sizing constraint, not a switch), and labels wrap/ellipsize. All of these are *parameter* adaptivity; GTK CSS has **no `@container`/media queries** (confirmed — nothing in the CSS parser), so the pure-CSS web approach we rejected earlier has literally no GTK analog.

## Why this matters for our design

GTK's own idiomatic answer to "narrow layout vs. wide layout" is **`GtkStack` + the app deciding** — i.e., exactly the app-side selection model. But you deliberately chose the other model: *only the selected child is transmitted + the renderer measures and derives the fit locally*. That model is **genuinely additive to GTK** — it requires the renderer to observe its own allocation, a capability GTK4 withholds (no signal, no CSS container queries, no auto-fit container). On the web the browser hands us `ResizeObserver` + CSS `@container` for free; on GTK we must build the observation ourselves — which is precisely the ~40-line tick-callback (or subclass `allocate`) seam we discussed.

So: no, it's not that GTK4 is missing "visual reactivity" — it's that its reactivity is parent-imposed, constraint-based, and app-selected, and our chosen semantics live outside all three.

Is it the same issue with swiftui, jet compose and qt?

Good comparison to draw. The short answer: **same *problem*, but three of the four frameworks ship a native answer built into their layout engine — GTK4 is the outlier.** Here's the per-toolkit reality:

## SwiftUI — **has the feature natively**
`ViewThatFits` is a first-party layout container (iOS 16+/macOS 13+). Because SwiftUI **owns measurement**: a view answers `sizeThatFits(_ proposal:)` with its ideal size, and the layout engine proposes sizes and picks the first child that fits — no signal, no polling, no window. `GeometryReader` additionally hands a view its own size for custom adaptive layouts. "Only the pick renders" is inherent (it's a layout decision).

## Jetpack Compose — **has the feature natively**
Same story: `androidx.compose.foundation.layout.ViewThatFits` (Compose 1.5+) is a `Layout` that measures children against the incoming `Constraints` and keeps the first that fits; `BoxWithConstraints` exposes the parent constraints (`maxWidth`) for hand-written breakpoints. Measurement is engine-owned, so the pick is just a measurement pass, and size changes re-run composition/layout — no observer plumbing needed.

## Qt — **observability is easy; no auto-fit primitive**
two flavors:
- **QtWidgets**: unlike GTK4, it kept a per-widget resize notification — **`QWidget::resizeEvent(QResizeEvent*)`** is a real native callback (GTK4's missing primitive exists here). Switching between layouts is app-driven (`QStackedLayout`/`QStackedWidget`), like GTK, but observing your own size is trivial.
- **Qt QML**: size *is* a reactive property — `width`/`height` are bindable, so "react to my own width" is idiomatic (`width >= 640 ? wide : narrow`, `onWidthChanged`). There's no named `ViewThatFits`, but the pattern is a few binding lines rather than framework machinery.

## GTK4 — **the genuine outlier**
No size-change signal, no measurement-owned "pick" primitive, no `@container`/media-query CSS. Its reactivity is parent-imposed + constraint-based + app-selected — so both the *observation* (tick/subclass) **and** the *selection* (the app) are on you.

## The underlying reason

| Toolkit | Owns measurement? | Auto-fit primitive | Own-size observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| SwiftUI | yes (layout engine) | `ViewThatFits` ✓ | engine proposals |
| Compose | yes (measure pass) | `ViewThatFits` ✓ | `Constraints`/`BoxWithConstraints` |
| Qt QML | reactive props | none (but trivial via bindings) | `width` bindable ✓ |
| QtWidgets | no | none | `resizeEvent()` ✓ |
| GTK4 | no | none | ✗ (removed signal; tick/subclass) |

Frameworks that **own measurement and layout** (SwiftUI, Compose) can offer automatic fit natively, because "which child fits" is a layout decision *inside* their engine. The widget-toolkit family (GTK4, QtWidgets) hands layout to negotiation instead, so auto-fit is outside the toolkit — and GTK4 additionally stripped the size notification, making it the only one where even *observing* the size is extra work. That's exactly why our "renderer measures + transmits only the selected child" design feels native on web (`ResizeObserver`+`@container`), SwiftUI, and Compose, but has to be built on GTK4.

## Plan — remove SizeThatFits from the GTK renderer + document in status.md

**`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs`** (revert these additions):
1. Remove `use gtk::prelude::WidgetExt;` (line 46 — added only for `connect_size_allocate`).
2. Remove the `fit_states` field (+ doc) from `GtkRenderer` and the `FitState` struct + its doc.
3. Remove `fit_states: HashMap::new(),` from the `Default` impl; remove `self.fit_states.remove(&id);` from `sync()`'s stale cleanup.
4. Remove the `SIZE_THAT_FITS` hook in `sync_node` (`if node.component_type == ... { self.sync_fit(id, &node); }`) and the entire `sync_fit` method.
5. Revert `widget_kind`'s Stack arm (drop `| component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS => WidgetKind::Stack`) and `is_container` (drop the `| component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS`).

**`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/layout.rs`**: remove the `SIZE_THAT_FITS => Some(Orientation::Vertical)` arm (+ comment) from `stack_orientation`.

**`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/host.rs`**: remove the `value_type::LIST` branch in `SET_PROPERTY` decode and the `list_csv` helper (both added solely for `FIT_QUERY`). LIST properties then fall through to the generic raw-offset handling (the pre-feature behavior). The `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` boundary stays as fixed.

**`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/status.md`** (rewrite the committed gap note): state that **`SIZE_THAT_FITS` is NOT implemented in the GTK renderer** — the fit slot is unmapped (`widget_kind` → Blank), `FIT_QUERY` is not decoded, and no `FIT_CHANGED` is reported; the web (SSR + DOM) and Java DSL surfaces are implemented, and Rust-DSL/engine emit the constant surface, but GTK rendering is deferred because GTK4 has no size-change notification — a frame-clock tick observer (or a `GtkWidget` `allocate` override) is the future path.

Then commit the three reverted files + `status.md` on `feat/size-that-fits`. No other crate/surface is touched (core, wire, DSL-Java, DSL-Rust, web, golden stay).

content.text:
`com.pathland.view.*` covers `SizeThatFits`/`Fit` — no import change needed. Here's the plan.

## Plan — responsive Now-Playing sidebar (>600pt, via `SizeThatFits`)

**`MusicPlayerView.java` (`body()`)** — wrap the outer row in a `SizeThatFits` fit slot whose **two candidates are the whole row layouts** (so the slot's measured width = the parent row's / window width — exactly "parent > 600"):

- Extract the main play area (the big `ZStack`: `LibraryView` + floating `PlayerBar` + lyric pill) into a `View mainArea`.
- `View wideRow = HStack.of(mainArea, new NowPlayingSidebar(...).with(Clipped.of())).with(FrameMod.of(FILL, FILL));`
- `return SizeThatFits.of(Fit.of(wideRow, 600f), Fit.any(mainArea)).with(FrameMod.of(FILL, FILL)).with(AccessibilityRole.of(Roles.MAIN));`
- Below 600 the slot transmits **only** the compact `mainArea` (no sidebar subtree at all); at ≥600 the `FIT_CHANGED` from the DOM's `ResizeObserver` → the server's fit sink swaps in the wide row. Because `mainArea` sits at index 0 in both candidates, the reconcile **reuses** the `LibraryView`/`PlayerBar`/lyric nodes and only inserts/removes the sidebar subtree.

**`MusicPlayerViewTest.java`** — the mount now defaults to the **compact** candidate, so:
- Update `libraryRendersTracksAndAlbumArt`: the initial frame still renders library/covers, but **"Now Playing" is absent**; assert `Components.SIZE_THAT_FITS` present, then drive the real path — `result.fitInputs()` → `accept(1)` → a new frame that now contains the sidebar ("Now Playing" header, `SIDEBAR_BG`, etc.).
- `playerBarRendersTransportAndSliders` stays green untouched (audio/player live inside `mainArea`, present in both candidates).

**Behavioral notes**

content.text:
Done — committed as `c517d28b` on `feat/size-that-fits`.

**`MusicPlayerView`** now wraps the main row in a `SizeThatFits` slot:
- **≥600pt** → `Fit.of(rowWithSidebar, 600f)` — `mainArea + NowPlayingSidebar`
- **<600pt** → `Fit.of(mainArea)` — compact, sidebar subtree **not transmitted**

The shared `mainArea` (library + floating player bar + lyric pill) sits at index 0 in both candidates, so the reconcile re-uses those nodes and only inserts/removes the sidebar on a `FIT_CHANGED` swap (driven by the DOM client's `ResizeObserver` → fit sink).

**Tests** (31 demo tests green): `libraryRendersTracksAndAlbumArt` now expects the sidebar to start hidden and asserts the `SIZE_THAT_FITS` slot; new `fitShowsTheSidebarWhenTheParentIsWideEnough` drives `result.fitInputs()→accept(1)` and verifies the sidebar + "Up Next" render. `MusicPlayerViewTest.playerBarRendersTransportAndSliders` untouched (audio/player live in `mainArea`). Verified with `mvn -pl pathland-demo-views test` and a full `mvn install`.

On a wide window you'll see the compact row at first paint, then the sidebar swaps in once the client has measured — the intended "only the selected child transmits" behavior. (GTK desktop keeps the compact layout, as documented.) To see it live, restart the Spring/Quarkus demo and resize past 600px.
